Counselor: A car accident?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What happened?
Client: Well, we were at a stop sign, and I was, like, actually a red light, and there was one car here, another car here, and then I was here, and the car was behind, coming up behind me, and then they hit me, and then I hit the car in front of me.
Counselor: Oh, yeah? You okay?
Client: I kind of, you know, you know.

Client: Yeah, yeah.

And I was kind of, like, maybe not. Like, I'm kind of, like, hesitant to get back in the car.
Counselor: So when he said that about the trip, what was the thought that came in your mind?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, mister Urban. It's nice to see you again. From our previous session, I know you spoke about the relationship you and your wife were going through. In the bad terms, she got left off. So I want to ask you, what would make you cheat on your wife?
Client: You know, I've been asked that question every day for the past two, three weeks. And the only thing I can respond with is what would make a wife cheat on her husband? I mean, it's petty. I know it's petty. But I loved her. And finding out that more than once she was with somebody else, that took something from me that I couldn't get back. And for months I was dealing with. What could I have done? What was it? What did I do? Because it has to have been me. She's too nice a person for that, right? She's too smart a person for that, right? And then weeks of me finally understanding that it wasn't me. A decision that you make is a decision that you make. So when Susie, my administrative assistant, came into the picture, I had a decision that I had to make. I have to take it off and spend time with Susie. Or keep it on and spend many a night alone. So why? You figure it out.
Counselor: So do you think that you did it for revenge? Were you trying to get back at your wife?
Client: I guess. I mean, what else could it be? Yeah, maybe I am that petty. But it's just. It's not love anymore.
Counselor: So why are you still in a marriage, mister Urban? If it's not love, if it's not for love, why do you feel that you must stay in America?
Client: Because that's the type of household I was brought up in.
Counselor:
output: Explain that to me.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Lisa. How you doing today?
Client: I'm good, but there has been an issue, you know, we've been working on, like, my motivation.
Counselor: Sure.
Client: Well, kind of. It's kind of related to that. So I'm in school, and every few weeks we have, like, papers to write, and I know, I know it. I know I can do it. It's just actually sitting down and doing it.
Counselor: All right, well, tell me about the papers.
Client: Well, they're usually about five pages long. And I just look at it, and I'm like, it's five pages. But I'm like, okay. So I go sit down, you know, at my computer. I'm like, all right, I'm gonna start on references. Mm hmm. So I get, you know, I start off good. I do the references, but then it's like I get sidetracked so easily, and then I end up killing, like, 2 hours checking the news. Checking. And then it goes to my phone, and then just looking up recipes. I mean, it gets really off topic. And then I realize, you know, I haven't done anything.
Counselor: All right, so you. You have a five page paper. You sit down to work on it. You have the references. You get that part taken care of, but then it sounds like you kind of wander off a little bit.
Client: Oh, big time.
Counselor: Yeah. Okay, and then what happens after you are done wandering a little bit?
Client: Well, I get kind of annoyed with it, and then I'm like, well, you know, I've already, you know, it's already night time. I'll try and try to do it tomorrow. And then, you know, either tomorrow doesn't happen or the same thing happens, and it's just. And then I end up, you know, rushing right at the end of, you know, due tomorrow, and I'm getting all these five pages done. It's really hard for me.
Counselor: So you are, you are finishing the assignment on time? So the problem isn't lateness?
Client: No. I mean, I get it done.
Counselor: You get it done.
Client: It's just all at the last minute.
Counselor: So it's really the, how the time breaks out isn't working out well for you?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: You'd rather not be doing it at the last moment?
Client: No. I mean, I try not to. I mean, I set time aside to go sit down. I'm like, all right, you know, we're going to start on this paper, then sidetracked. I'm watching tv. I'm on my phone. I'm on some other website.
Counselor:
output: So these, so these activities that you're engaging in between when you start the work and before you start writing. So, gathering the references before you start writing, you said check an email. Yeah, and other kind of. It sounds like unplanned, small activities.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: So these daggy little sheets we use for cognitive behavioral therapy or strategies. And you can see at the top they talk about the situation, and down the bottom they talk about the feelings, and in between, there's a whole lot of discussion about the thoughts. Yeah. So again, it's sort of easier with a concrete example. So I might get you to write in, if you're happy, to, the situation that you mentioned, the tram situation in the little situation box there.
Client: Of course.
Counselor: Okay, so what have you written in there?
Client: Catching the tram.
Counselor: Okay, so what feelings do you have when you go to catch the tram? And just before you tell me, often it's useful to have sort of one word for a feeling, something that's really in your gut rather than a long expression. So what's your feeling?
Client: Anxious. That's the one. Anxious.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: That's the one.
Counselor: Do you want to write that in and see? Are there any other feelings that really resonate with you? I mean, that's enough. But is there anything other sort of feeling you have when you're
Client: scared?
Counselor: Okay, so pop that one in there. Anything else?
Client: Embarrassed.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: All right.
Counselor: Do you want to pop that one in there as well? This is great. You've really sort of clicked with it. All right, so now why are we doing all this? Because what I'm going to ask you now is to imagine what the little voice in your head, you know, that little self talk is saying when you're feeling anxious. So what are you feeling anxious about? What's the sort of story in your head that's going on there?
Client: All right, I'm. How's it. What happens? I'm thinking I'm gonna get lost.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Yeah. So I'm anxious because I think I'm gonna get lost.
Counselor: Okay. So do you want to write that one down?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. I'm worried I'll get lost.
Client: Yep.
Counselor: See, it's a bit artificial bringing it up, but there's sort of a point to all this.
Client: Yeah, yeah, no, I get it. It's good to actually think through what exactly.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: Happens.
Counselor: Okay, so you said you're anxious because you're worried or get lost. Any other thoughts? That sort of self talk?
Client: Um, yeah, I reckon I start blushing and, you know, going red.
Counselor: Right. Okay. It's another good one to write down. Do you want to write that one down in the thoughts as word? Brilliant. Okay, and so what have you written there?
Client: Panic that I'll go red. Blush.
Counselor: Okay. All right. Got it.
Client: I do.
Counselor: So this is sort of really useful. We've been able to sort of tease out your situation, the feelings. And really, what's that little voice in your head that's going on? Now, there's been a point to all this because what we do with this CBT approach is we try and challenge some of these thoughts. Okay.
Client: Because I know they're, you know, silly. I know that.
Counselor: Yeah. I mean, some of our thoughts are realistic, some of them are correct and. And some of them aren't realistic and not very helpful. And. And it sounds like these ones that are sort of causing problems for you. So, so what I'm going to do, let's look at this first one here. You've said, I'm worried I'll get lost. Okay? So let's just look at the evidence for that. So I'm gonna be a little bit like a lawyer here and so let's look at the evidence for that. Or not. So you say, don't worry, don't get lost. Have you ever been lost in the city?
Client: No, I don't think I have.
Counselor: Yeah. Okay. Do you usually know which tram to get on?
Client: Oh, yeah, I make sure I know because I'm so scared I'm gonna get lost. I make sure I know all the numbers of the trams, where they go. So, yeah, actually. So I've never got lost.
Counselor: Okay. All right. So in some ways, how likely do you think it really is that you're actually going to get lost? I know you're having that thought, but.
Client: Well, it's actually really unlikely.
Counselor: Fantastic. And so what I'll get you to write in this little right hand column here is it's really unlikely I'm going to get lost. Okay, so these are what we sort of call disputing thoughts or, you know, alternative ways of looking at it that a little bit fairer to ourselves and a little bit more realistic. That's fantastic.
Client: So unlikely I will get lost.
Counselor: Yeah. It's actually unlikely, isn't it? Yeah. Have a look at the next one. I'll panic and I'll blush and everyone will look at me. Okay, so let's just have a little look at that. If you did get a bit panicky, do you think people would really be noticing?
Client: Probably not. Maybe not.
Counselor:
output: Well, let's put it another way. Do you look at other people on the tram and sort of decide whether or not they look emotionally happy or sad or panicky?

output: So you have some uncertainty around what you want to do with your majority. I'm wondering, what are your thoughts when you're talking to your father? About that.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Miss Payne. My name is Rebecca, and I will be your therapist today. And I see on your notes that you prefer to be called Kelly. Is that correct?
Client: Yes, ma'am. My name is Kelly, but a lot of people call me Kelly Joe. They do? Yeah. My papa in particular. He likes to call me Joe. Kelly Joe. I was named after my great grandfathers.
Counselor: Okay, well, would you prefer that I call you Kelly or Kelly Joe?
Client: No, just call me Kelly. I think Kelly Joe is really country. Okay, we'll just go with Kelly.
Counselor: All right, Kelly. The first thing I want to do is I'm going to explain our roles that we have today in our session. And of course, you know, as I said, I'm your therapist, but you're also actively participating in this session. And anytime you have a question, if you have any comments, if you don't understand something, I want you to tell me so that I can make sure that you understand everything that we're doing, that we're talking about, and it will be actively. Yeah. Between both of us will be a team, if you want.
Client: Oh, I definitely ask questions. Trust me. I like to ask a lot of questions. I like to talk.
Counselor: Well, that's good. And then the other thing, we have an agenda that I'm going to try to stick by. We want to start off with a mood check. I'll just kind of see how you're feeling today. We'll talk about your presenting problems, and we'll go into making some goals, and I'll explain a little bit of the theory that I use for our sessions. Kind of do a little educational piece to make sure you understand what's going on, and we'll give a summary. And also, I may have some homework that we can talk about.
Client: Okay. Because I sure do have lots of problems. I can tell you about tons of problems.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: So I'm going to be talking your ears off.
Counselor: Well, we have approximately about 15 to 20 minutes today, and I'll let you know when the time starts to run short so you're not taken by surprise.
Client: Okay, that will be fine. But if I need more time, I'll just have to buy it, I guess.
Counselor: Well, we can work something out, I'm sure.
Client: Well, I'll try to keep it short.
Counselor: Okay. Well, the first thing I do want to do is check on your mood and just kind of see how you're feeling today.
Client: Well, today, I just tell you, that teenager of mine, I could just hang him up by his toes. That right there. If I could just get that settled for a while. I think I might have get some common ground with him. I think I might be okay.
Counselor: Okay. So you would say you're kind of feeling frustrated.
Client: I'm frustrated and stressed and can't sleep. Just, you know, really just snappy. I just snap at him all the time.
Counselor: Okay. And I guess the biggest thing would be your frustration. On a scale of one to ten with your frustration, how would you rate that?
Client: Why? Twelve, of course. Yeah. Frustration with a teenage boy. Have you ever said girls are hard to raise? Boys, they're hard to raise.
Counselor: Okay. So you're really having some frustration issues. And I noticed you mentioned your sleep that you're not sleeping very well.
Client: No, not sleeping well. I think I'm just stressed with him all the time and just, you know, just the day to day life stuff. And I'm just stressed. Just stressed. Not sleeping really good at all.
Counselor: And it seems like maybe not sleeping, you know, a lot of times that can also add to you're being more prone to de stressed. So that's something we need to kind of get balanced out. So you're getting the sleep that you need, but you're also able to, you know, deal with your teenager, deal with your child and kind of get to where you need to be.
Client: That would be great. That would be great. I've got to get some sleep.
Counselor: So you said that you're very frustrated or stressed out. And that kind of leads me right into, you know, the main reason that you're here today to presenting problems. And I know you didn't mention it has to do with your teenager, but can you clarify a little bit about what's going on with him?
Client: I think it's racing hormones.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: He just can't. Anything that I say, he just disagrees. You know, he's right, I'm wrong. We can't come to common ground on anything. Curfew. He's just, you know, I feel I give him everything and he feels that we're too strict, you know? You know, and he wants to do things that I don't feel that is appropriate. But who knows? Just, who knows? What is he, what is he really wanting? But we've got. We've got to come to some type of common ground to figure out what we can do. Just make our life just a little bit easier and not fight all the time.
Counselor: So it sounds to me y'all have a lot of little things that y'all disagree on, but it's all added up to be a very big stressor.
Client: Oh, yes. I could just hang him up by his toenails okay.
Counselor: Okay. Well, let me remind you that I am a mandated reporter. So anything that you say, if it is something that would leave me of concern, I do have to make a report.
Client: Well, hate him, but by his toenails. I'll just tell you what.
Counselor: Okay, so I know you said you have some communication problems. I believe I heard you say that.
Client: We do.
Counselor: Okay. And do you feel that maybe it's just he's not listening or that y'all just.
Client: We just can't agree.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: We just can't agree.
Counselor:
output: Okay.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Marcy, how you doing?
Client: I've been better.
Counselor: Been better. Yeah, I saw that you called a few times between the last session and today. You left a few messages.
Client: Yeah, I was trying to get holding you. I had something I really needed to discuss with you, but nobody called me back. I emailed you a couple times, I never got a reply, so I was just wondering what's going on with that?
Counselor: We can talk about that. I want to talk about that after getting those messages. Remember we discussed the process for when your mood deteriorates and you had a few other resources you wanted to connect with before calling me.
Client: Yeah, I kind of remember it.
Counselor: Your brother was one of those resources.
Client: Oh, yeah, that's useless anyway. Go on.
Counselor: Did you attempt to.
Client: No, he's so busy with it, like he could never help me. I don't think he even cares what I'm going through. He's got his own stuff to deal with, he's got his own family and all this stuff and. Yeah, he doesn't care.
Counselor: So you didn't contact him first because he thought he doesn't care? Yeah, and we'd also talked about a few different friends that you had that you'd reached out to, you didn't contact them or did.
Client: Well, I did call my one friend, Beth, but I. She was like, oh, can I call you back? And of course she didn't because nobody ever calls me back. You know, I'm like, they all have their own lives. No one really cares what I'm doing. You know, it's always like that. So that's why I thought I could reach out to you since you're supposed to be helping me, but apparently you never call me back or answer any of my emails, so.
Counselor: Right. We talked about how there's limitations on time and how it would be better if we could keep the therapy in here in person. Right. And not get really too excessive with the telephone calls. I realize that when you're in distress, there's that kind of feeling that it would be a good idea to call. But remember, we discussed different levels of distress. And if it's something common that you've been through before and you kind of know the outcome, connecting with one of those resources might be more helpful.
Client: Yeah, I just feel like you're the only one that can help me, you know, I mean, my boyfriend, like, things aren't going well with him. I thought he could help me, but I guess he can't. And I think he's running around on me and all that. So I was just like, well, let me reach out to doctor Grande and see if it can help me, because it seems like my last resort.
Counselor: I remember you discussing, a few weeks ago, your boyfriend, and you had a fairly high opinion of him. Like, it was. It seemed like a positive.
Client: Yeah, he was great. He was great. And then, you know, he was in the other room and he got a text message, and I was like, let me just look at that. Because I was just curious to see what's going on with him because he never talks to me about anything. And so I looked at it, and it was a girl's name and number that I don't know. And so he came back in. You know, they put it away quickly, and I didn't say anything, like, what's wrong with you? Because I was acting weird and I was like, nothing. So then he went out, so I followed him. And then he went to, like, some friend's house. And I don't know if there's girls there or not, but. So I kind of think he's running around, maybe. I don't know. And I can't trust him. I can't trust anybody, you know? So I don't know. I mean, he was so awesome before, but now I just don't know. But he was everything I ever wanted.
Counselor: Yeah, I remember. You seem very excited about where that relationship could go.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you seem like you're much more negative about.
Client: Yeah. I mean, if he's not going to be faithful to me, what am I supposed to do? Yeah, I mean, it's just like every other guy that I've ever dated, like, either leave me or cheat on me or lie to me. So, I mean, I don't know why I thought this one was going to be different. Seriously, why would this one be different?
Counselor: So you have. You had this experience with the text message and you don't know? You don't know any more than that? But it sounds like you kind of jumped to, he's cheating. So, you know, he went to a text message and went to someone's house.
Client: Yeah. I don't know if they were related. The text message and him leaving, I mean, but I just assumed. So I'm just gonna assume because it seems to be a pattern in my life. You know, everybody lets me down.
Counselor: Could it be that you're jumping to that conclusion prematurely?
Client: Probably, but I guess it's all I know that's all. I've always been treated, so I kind of feel like, why would this be different? Even though I thought it was in the beginning, but I don't know.
Counselor: So you feel like you've seen this all before, this pattern?
Client: Yeah, I guess I just always pick the wrong people or it's probably just me. I think I'm the one that's just unlovable. I've been told that growing up a lot. So I think it's me because he's great. I mean, he's great and he's good looking, he has a good job. And I always thought I'm like, why is he with me? And then now I see, like, he doesn't really want to be with me. Whoever he was texting, that's probably the person wants to be with him. She's probably, like, pretty and has, she probably has a good job and she's got everything going for her and so.
Counselor: So you really, this week at least, you don't seem to think a lot of yourself.
Client: No. I mean, when things are going bad in my relationships, they really seem to get to me, you know?
Counselor: So in a way, you feel like your mood is subject to how your current romantic relationship is going?
Client: Yeah, I guess that's pretty right on. Yeah, I would say that.
Counselor: Is there anything that you can do from your side to improve what's going on?
Client: No, I don't think so. I think it's everybody else that is treating me wrong, you know? So unless I find the right person who's going to treat me right, then I don't know what I'm going to do. So.
Counselor: So the. So the key to feeling better is finding the right person.
Client: Yeah, I think so. And like I said, I thought he was the right one in the beginning, and now I don't know anymore. But, you know, I really don't want him to leave me because, like, then when I gotta do him, now I'm gonna be alone. I want to be alone because I love him, but, you know, so I think I probably will forgive him and just stay with them because I don't want to be alone. I'm too scared to do that. I mean, I don't want to be alone without somebody. You know, I really need somebody. Yes.
Counselor: So does some of this seem like what you're describing with your mood, does some of this seem like you're out of control?
Client: Yeah, because I feel like I can't control other people's actions, and that really makes me mad. That makes me really angry, you know? That what am I supposed to do? And so I think acting out and following them and checking their text messages, and it's the only thing that makes me feel in control, I guess. I don't know.
Counselor: I know in the past, when we've talked about this, you've mentioned that you thought that that behavior could be driving them away, too.
Client: Yeah, I mean, I can see that. I mean, people want, you know, some that they can trust, too. And I'm not sure I've always been honest with them, but I'm always looking for things that they're gonna do to manipulate me or try to, like, you know, screw me over or whatever. So here's my guard down. Yeah, I'm suspicious.
Counselor: I wonder if sometimes you acting on those suspicions, that's not making things a little worse in those relationships.
Client: Yeah, probably. But, I mean, like I said before, I don't want to be alone. I don't want to move out somebody. I need somebody. I need somebody. I need somebody to be with, you know, I need someone to help me with things. I don't want to be alone. instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Okay. Ali, welcome back to our session today.
Client: Hi.
Counselor: Hi. How are you? How are you doing today?
Client: I'm fine, thank you.
Counselor: Good. Have you gotten up to anything interesting today or this week?
Client: Well, yeah, I want to talk specifically about a situation that I had with a home.
Counselor: Okay, that sounds great. So I'm just going to put a pin in that for a sec. We'll put that on our agenda. Before that, let's just talk, do a bit of a check in. Would you say that your mood today, I know we're working on some depression and anxiety, some lower mood. Would you say that your mood is about the same as last week? Better or worse than last week?
Client: A little bit better.
Counselor: A little bit better?
Client: A little bit better. But when I start thinking about all my negative stuff, brings me a little bit down.
Counselor: Yeah, well, and that makes sense, doesn't it, given we talked about the link between our thoughts and our moods. So when we start thinking about that negative stuff, it starts pulling us down. But I'm actually curious about. You said, I wrote down here that you're feeling a little bit better. What do you think is happening in your life that's bringing you to feel a little bit better?
Client: I think that with the homework, like realizing the cognitive distortions, that I was able to understand that I'm seeing everything very negative.
Counselor: Okay. Yeah. So you're kind of seeing that as something that happens for you quite often?
Client: Yeah, yeah, yeah.
Counselor: And what does that. What kind of. What does that mean for you? Or how are you then? Why does that make you feel better?
Client: Well, you talked last session about seeing everything through the dark lenses and remove those lenses. So I have been trying to remove and say, okay, probably I'm being very negative and try to switch it slowly. Oh, good.
Counselor: That's fantastic. So interesting that we were talking about this link between our thoughts and our moods and that you really have felt. When we think about the negative stuff, obviously our mood goes down and you've been working at trying to look at more positive things, and your mood is going up. So that's really interesting and great. Okay. And thanks for bringing up the homework. Last week, you and I decided that you were going to kind of pay attention to your cognitive distortions and kind of track them. What did you learn?
Client: I learned that, as I said, I'm seeing everything very negative, but I play a lot with. I should.
Counselor: I should. Okay. Do you know why? A bad therapy joke for shoulds?
Client: No.
Counselor: You want to be careful not to should all over yourself. Right. So, okay, wonderful that you're noticing not wonderful that you're doing this, but good that you're noticing you're doing a lot of shoulds. How do you think noticing that plays into your mood?
Client: I think that put out, it puts a lot of pressure, because then you should be like, you should be perfect. You should not be depressed. You should not feel anxious. But still you are depressed or you are anxious, right?
Counselor:
output: Yeah. So I like the way you talked about that is those pressure words, right? The shoulds, the oughts, the musts. When we find ourselves doing that a lot, as I talked about last time, that's a real opportunity for you to breathe and take a step back from that negative thinking and think, is there something that I can think that's more positive or helpful for me in this way?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Okay, Marsha, so how can I help you today?
Client: Well, I'm working full time. I'm a part time student. I've just gotten engaged, and I live at home. There's just so much stress in my life. I have everything happening all at once. Just to top it all off, I failed an exam, a really big exam, and I just feel like I can't do anything anymore. I can't do anything right. I've just got so much stress, and I feel like such a disappointment, such a failure. And I've embarrassed my family by failing. I just don't know what to do anymore. I guess I've come here today to tell you, like, I want to leave uni, and I guess that's why I've come here to you today.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like a whole lot of stuff's on top of you at the moment.
Client: Yeah, just so much. Just all parting on. Yeah.
Counselor: So you're working full time, plus part time study. Part time study. And then you've got your wedding preparation.
Client: Yeah, just got engaged, and weddings just a month away now, so, yeah, so I've just got so much happening. Work is really, really demanding and. Yeah, just fail this exam. It's just. Yeah, don't know what to do all too much.
Counselor: So imagine you've been sweating on this for a while, and it's all been swirling around in your head.
Client: Just been building up and building up and so much pressure with everything. And I'm living at home, so my parents, you know, a lot of pressure, need to do everything right. And. Yeah, by failing this, I feel like I've just embarrassed and disappointed them, and I just don't feel like I'm good enough, you know, to go on studying.
Counselor: Okay. And have they said much to you about failing your exam?
Client: They haven't said much. I was really scared to tell them, actually, because I knew they'd just be so disappointed and just embarrassed by the fact that I did fail. Yeah. I've never failed anything before. And so, yeah, really hard.
Counselor: Yeah. So it's new and you don't like it at all?
Client: Not at all, no. And I think leaving uni will just be the way out, just so I don't have to go through it again.
Counselor: Right. Okay. Well, I'm glad you've come to counselling, because it's good for us to get an outsider's opinion when we've got so much on our plate and we're confused as to what to do and our emotions can get in the way. And you've just said earlier that a whole lot of stuff's on your plate at the moment. Okay. So I'm glad you've come here. Here at the clinic, we use the ABC model, which is a cognitive behavioural therapy model. So, Marsha, some counsellors have put together a list of beliefs that we often use and we don't realise that we're using those beliefs and they tend to be faulty ones. Here's the list. Here, have a look through that to see if there are any beliefs that you might be operating on at the moment.
Client: I think number two.
Counselor: Okay, read that one out for me.
Client: That it's necessary to have a high degree of order uncertainty in order to be happy and perform well.
Counselor: Yeah, yeah, you mentioned that earlier.
Client: Number four, that it's necessary to be competent and successful in all those things which are attempted.
Counselor: Yeah, that's an expectation from your family.
Client: Yeah, possibly. Number eight, that life should be entirely pleasant and enjoyable and that any frustration, discomfort or pain would be unbearable.
Counselor: Which one of those stands out the most for you at the moment?
Client: Um, probably number four.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: How would you put that in your own words?
Client: That I need to be successful all the time in everything that I do. Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. And is that different from what's happening in your life at the moment?
Client: Well, failing that exam, I mean, I wasn't successful with that. So. Yeah, I mean, it just throws out, I guess, even number two because throws out all the order in my life. I need to have everything, you know? So I need to know what I'm doing, where I'm going. Yeah.
Counselor: So, okay, so if number four is an expectation that your family have and that you have of yourself, how do you measure up next to number four?
Client: I don't feel like I'm good enough.
Counselor: Okay. All right. I. Well, what I'd like to do is put some of those ideas on the board under the ABC and I'll explain as we go along.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Okay. So what do you think the trigger point might be or the activating event for you at the moment?
Client: I mean, there are a lot of things, but I think obviously failing the exam was the main one.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right. And the consequences. You thinking of leaving uni?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right. And that statement you made earlier about.
Client: I'm not good enough?
Counselor:
output: Yeah, that's. That's the b one. That's the crucial one. And I'll explain it shortly when I get up to the board.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Jean. How are you?
Client: I'm good.
Counselor: So this is the second time that we've seen each other. Right. You came in for the initial assessment about a week ago now, I think, and I got to know you and your history and kind of the symptoms that you've been dealing with, and it seems like you've been struggling with depression. Is that. Does that sound right?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Yeah. So between, you know, last time you were here and now, did anything come up, anything positive, anything challenging?
Client: Yes. When I try to pull weeds, it just takes me forever in my garden, and then I have to come in and sit down, and then I just don't understand why I can't do it like I used to, and it's frustrating.
Counselor: Okay. So is that. That's related to the medical issues that.
Client: Yes. I have arthritis in my knees and my back.
Counselor: How long has that been going on for?
Client: Oh, really bad for the last, like three years. So.
Counselor: And that's been kind of a difficult adjustment. You were really active before, right?
Client: Yes. I could do all my gardening one day and not have to stop. And now I have to stop. And it's.
Counselor: So what do you think about all that?
Client: I hate it. It's like, why? Why can't I do it? You know?
Counselor: Yeah. Yeah. Well, it is. It's a big difference when you are, you know, not experiencing physical pain and you can do all these things that you enjoy and then something happens, you know, as we're getting older, it always does. So, yeah, it can definitely present a lot of challenges. Anything else happened in the last week?
Client: Well, I've been wanting. I need to go walking more often, and I just can't. It just bothers me, my knees and. And I get frustrated because I can't do that and.
Counselor: Okay. And then, you know, when you get frustrated and you can't do something, what do you do after that?
Client: I, um, just sit there and usually get up and eat something, and that's not good for me when I'm trying to lose weight. So then.
Counselor: Oh, I see. So it's kind of like a cycle. You want to do good things for your health and exercise, but it's been challenging because of your medical issues. And then it kind of leads you to overeating, which is kind of counterintuitive to your goals.
Client: Right. It's like, why. Why am I eating this?
Counselor: Well, you may have noticed that I ask a lot of questions about what you think about things and how you feel about things. You know, in the first session you came in, and then today I just kind of wanted to point out how cognitive behavioral therapy works. That's the kind of therapy that I actually do and will be using together to kind of hopefully help you get through this time to where you feel like there's some improvement in your mood and how you're feeling. So let me just start by drawing a little diagram using an example that we just talked about together. So say a situation comes up like, you go to pull the weeds in the garden. I'm going to write pull the weeds in the garden. And then you said you were able to do it, but for a short period of time before pain kind of got in the way. Right. And then when that pain got in the way, what was the thought that you had?
Client: It's like, why do I have this pain? Why? Before, I never did. I should be able to do this, but I can't.
Counselor: Okay. So I got, you know, why do I have this pain? And I should be able to do this. So then after you had that thought, what did you feel? What emotions came up for you?
Client: Frustrated, sad, and I get anxious.
Counselor: Okay. And then after you felt those things, the frustrated, sad, and anxious, that's when.
Client: I would eat the ice cream.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Our sweets, candy, whatever.
Counselor: Okay. So I kind of put this in a model to show you how cognitive behavioral therapy works. So all these different situations happen, and different people see them in different ways. So when you had, you know, this situation come up where you went to go pull the weeds in the garden and you couldn't do it as long as you wanted to, you had this kind of, like, more negative, self critical thought going on. I mean, you were able to go pull some of the weeds even if you weren't able to do as much as you wanted to. But because, you know, you kind of had these negative thoughts, it led you, it affected your emotions, and then in turn, it affected the behaviors that you did afterwards. And what we find in cognitive behavioral therapy is that we have the most control over our thoughts. You know, what we think of an event. Like I mentioned, we could think like, oh, well, you know, at least I was able to do this much. You know, I can give myself a rest. My body's telling me to take a rest, and then I can go back to it again. So that's kind of what our target is going to be. And it all starts with identifying these automatic thoughts that you're having, these quick reactions that are happening in your brain. And it seems very simple, but it is, you know, challenging to do. So that's what we're going to start off working on. Did that all make sense?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Okay, good. So I have this worksheet here that you can take with you and we'll get going on our first step in working together. So right here there's a lot of columns, but I really only want you to worry about the first three columns. And this is going to get you tracking what automatic thoughts are coming up for you. So we've got date and time, the situation or event that happened, and then automatic thoughts. So maybe we can go through one more because you did mention walking as well, right. That was also a challenge for you. So when was that you were going to go for a walk?
Client: Well, I was going to go yesterday and then I just. I just couldn't because my knees started. I just get out the door and can't even get down the steps sometimes.
Counselor: Oh, that must be difficult.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Right. And then I'm gonna put for the situation. Couldn't go for a walk. Alright. And then do you remember what thoughts you had?
Client: Looks like? Here's another thing I can't do.
Counselor: Okay. Any other thoughts that came into your head?
Client: Just frustrated because I should be able to do this. I always do it. I just used to walk a lot last year, not this year.
Counselor:
output: So I'm gonna write I should be able to do this. And actually when you said, you know, I was frustrated, that's more of what we call an emotion, which is the fourth box. We're not going to worry about that yet. We're just going to focus on identifying those thoughts. Now just keep this somewhere handy and then you can come check in a couple times a day and write down what you can remember. You don't have to be perfect with this. This is just to like, get us started. So does that seem like something that you could do over the next week?

Client: Yeah, yeah, definitely.
Counselor: You've had low mood in the past, but it's kind of. You've been able to pull yourself out of it before, but more recently you found that harder. Okay, so I understand that you first went to your GP. He referred you here about two months ago. Can I ask what led you to go to the GP in the first place?
Client: My long term boyfriend broke up with me and it was such a shock. Like, I really wasn't expecting it and it just got me really down and I just felt really lonely and I didn't really want to see people and just wanted to be in my own space. And my mum told me I should probably go to the doctors. Oh. And he's referred me to you.
Counselor: Okay. So it sounds then like you had that breakup and you weren't expecting it, so it kind of came out of the blue a bit and that you've been on your own quite a lot, so you've not been seeing people as much. And it sounds like your mum noticed that there's been a bit of a change in you. Okay. And how have things been then, since then, since that happened and since you went to the GP?
Client: I just. Nothing's really changed. Nothing's really improved. I just feel down, like everything's an effort and just feel distant from things. And like I said, I can't snap out of it.
Counselor: Okay. And how did you feel about coming here today?
Client: I was kind of disappointed in myself because I feel like nobody else my age is doing this. Like, I should have been able to snap out of it. Like, it's just another thing that I've not really. It's another thing that's making me stand out for the wrong reasons.
Counselor: Okay. So you feel like it's kind of odd or unusual to be coming to see a clinical psychologist? I suppose I just want to reassure you that it's absolutely normal to have feelings of depression and anxiety. It's really very common and it certainly isn't odd or strange at all. So it sounds like it was actually quite hard for you to come here today?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So what, I guess led you to do that? Because it sounds like maybe there was a lot pushing you against coming here today, but you've managed to come anyway.
Client: I'm just hoping that it's gonna help, I think. I didn't really want to admit it because it's just another failure, but my mum was talking to me and I know she's not really happy with the way I'm behaving. I didn't really want to disappoint her again and so I thought there's no harm in it, so she thought it'd come.
Counselor: So it sounds like partly you're doing it then, for your mum because you're a bit worried that she isn't pleased with you at the moment.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. Well, I think it's great that you've come here and definitely there's a lot of evidence to suggest that psychological therapy can help depression and particularly the type of therapy that we're going to be doing, which is called cognitive behaviour therapy. And I'll tell you a bit more about that as we go on, but I'm just trying to find out a bit more about you today. So I saw from your notes that you're a medic student.
Client: Yeah, I'm not currently in uni at the moment, but, yeah, last year as a medic student.

Client: It was pretty tough first year, so they then suggested that I took a year out. This is the break.

Client: Yeah, it was. I thought it's tough for everyone, but obviously we all take it in different ways, don't we?

Client: Yeah, I'm gonna have to. Really? So. Yeah.
Counselor: Don't sound too sure about that, though.
Client: I think returning is probably that's what's gonna make everyone happy. And I think, you know, at least I'll be able to finally achieve something and get something right, so. Yeah, like, next year I'm gonna. I'll get through it. Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. So it doesn't. It doesn't sound like you want to go back.
Client: I do. I do enjoy it. I just don't feel like me at the moment and I just. It's a lot of work and it's a lot of pressure, but that's what comes of it. And, you know, it'll work out for the best if I go.
Counselor: Okay. So I guess then there's quite a lot of thoughts and feelings about going back at the moment. I'm just wondering, in the meantime, what are you up to? What have you been doing?
Client: Well, I've not really had much on the horizon. My mum, her friend, owns a restaurant and she suggested that I did a bit of waitressing there just for a bit of money and stuff, because obviously I'm not in uni, so I've done that.

Client: Yeah.

Client: Um, last week, I think, um, I was thinking about what we talked about last week and I try to, you know, think about some things I want to work on and so it was better than before, but I still had a difficult time managing my work and my time and. Yeah.
Counselor: So have you, did you have any drinks last week?

Counselor: Good. So one of the things that we talked about was meeting with your professor or sending out an email to tell them how you, you need some assistance in completing your work because you have missed a lot of days from school.
Client: Yeah. Yeah, yeah. So I actually talked to my professor and asked him if I could get any extra help and he suggested to kind of reach out to the tutoring center that they, they have on campus. Client: Not really. I mean, it's pretty much the same pace. I'm very frustrated with the whole system. I'm working with inner city kids, african american kids, males in particular. You know, for the most part, we're talking about, you know, criminal arrest, drug abuse, you know, no education. And, you know, I don't know what I can really do for them anymore. Counselor: All right, so as you're working with these use, you're looking at their circumstances and you're saying the odds just don't look good for major improvement. That's leading you to lose hope in your ability to help them into different circumstances.
Client: Absolutely, yeah. I mean, it's just their reality. A kid comes in and mom is either dad's incarcerated, rotted, a picture. Mom is either on drugs or not fully engaged. And this kid has absolutely no life skills. None. He's self medicating or smoking marijuana. At the very least, it's marijuana. And he is just totally convinced that, you know, this is who he is the rest of his life. And he's sitting in front of me looking for answers, and I don't know if I have him.
Counselor: What kind of questions do they ask you?
Client: It's not even questions as more as it is just statements of, you know, this is my life, you know, the struggle is real. This is what I do, this is where I am. And, you know, anything other than this is not even, you know, I didn't fathom. So I'm sitting here, just kidding, I'm trying to draw him out of that whole mindset. But we're talking about years of social conditioning, years and years and years of it. And I just don't know if, you know, I have the skills and the tools to really break through that way of thinking.
Counselor: All right, so can you think of a particular case, particular youth that you're working with that, where you're finding the struggle. I just think of one particular individual where you're frustrated, you're making these statements that kind of. This is the way it is. They don't seem like they have much hope. You don't seem like they have much hope for them. Right. So you have one in mind.
Client: Yes, they do.
Counselor: Okay, so what's his self statement? What's he saying to you that you think is getting a reaction from you?
Client: That he's a drug dealer. He's going to continue to be a drug dealer. He's not going to stop. And that he's involved with gang activity, and that's his family. It's the only family he's ever known, and he's loyal to them. And that loyalty is deep. And he has absolutely no. Even the thought of going back to prison doesn't shape this kid.
Counselor: Not afraid of that.
Client: Not afraid of it for them. Gerald is like going to the school courtyard. There's all his boys in jail. So I'm sitting here like, what in the hell am I doing here with this kid? You know, what kind of options do I give him when I don't even believe he has any at this point?
Counselor: So that's really your automatic thought, is I don't believe he has any options. That's what's going through your mind when he says things like he's involved in gang activity and wants to continue dealing drugs? That's your thought?
Client: That's my thought, yeah.
Counselor: There's no way out for him.
Client: I don't see it. I just don't. I really don't see it for him. You know, he's self medicating. He's giving dirty urine to the probation office. He doesn't care. The judge has given them pass after pass after pass. But the kid just seems intent to, you know, to live this life.
Counselor: So in a sense, your mood, the sadness, the frustration is linked to, for example, this use statements and his philosophy. So he's saying that success is not an option, as you would think of success.
Client: Right.
Counselor: And you're reacting to that, and your mood is moving because of that.
Client: Yes. Yes. And I mean, to a certain degree, I understand where he's coming from. I mean, I was raised with the understanding that you were born black. That's one strike. You were born male. That's two strikes. A criminal arrest record, that's it. Life is over. So to a certain degree, his perception is reality. So I can't disagree with him. But at the same time, this is my job. And I'm having a very difficult time trying to give this kidde any glimpse of hope, which I don't even think he really wants.
Counselor: So it's hard for you to give the hope, and I'm sure he's looking for the hope. And you can understand his situation in terms of being african american, being male and having the criminal record and how that seems to stack the deck severely against him.
Client: Severely, yeah. And that's nothing. I mean, there's some truth to that. I don't know. That criminal arrest record, a conviction in this country pretty much relegates you to a certain level of society, in my.
Counselor: Opinion, in terms of employment opportunities.
Client: In terms of employment opportunity and things like that. So to a certain degree, I understand where he's coming from. It's just an absolute sense of hopelessness that comes from this kid. He'll sit in front of me and he'll just laugh. He'll laugh about it like, Mister D, this is my life. Why are you tripping? Why do you care so much? So I'm just starting not to carry.
Counselor: So you're starting to mirror that approach, the approach he's using.
Client: Yes, I am.
Counselor:
output: So what's bothering you in all this? Not only the circumstances, the racism, the discrimination, the circumstances in with the criminal record, that all bothers you, but also you're bothered because you're losing hope for him.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.

Counselor: Doing well?

Client: She wants to go, like, six days, but, yeah, I'm not sure. With work and school and everything, I can make the full six days, and plus, I'm a little nervous to go that long.
Counselor: So that's a long time for you.
Client: It is, yes.
Counselor: So when did you discover this trip.
Client: Was going to be actually last? Just a few days ago. She messaged me and said, hey, you want to go with me? And we'll go golfing and swimming? I love golfing. Like, you know, I want to go, but I just have these, just, you know, a little nervous about leaving.

Counselor: All right, so you had two kind of conflicting thoughts, right. So one. One is, I could never go that long. Six days, way too long. And the other one is, that would be enjoyable. You enjoy that?
Client: Absolutely, yeah.
Counselor: So which way are you leaning right now?
Client: I want to go to go, but maybe not for six days. Maybe just like a long weekend.
Counselor: Three, four days.
Client: Two would be ideal, but two would probably be idea, but two or three days. Yeah.
Counselor: So what do you think is causing this worry about being gone more than two days?
Client: I don't know. I mean, I've always, as a late teenager in my twenties, I've always had just nervous to leave home. As much as I love being home, I love to travel, too, and do different things. It's just, I guess I'm just afraid something to happen when I'm not around.
Counselor: So you're afraid something will happen to your house or.
Client: Well, I have pets, so I worry about them. My parents are getting older, so I worry about them mainly, like, my immediate family, mainly, I guess, my dad, because he's had a history of heart attacks, and then my pets, that's just worry something will happen. I won't be there.
Counselor: And how about when you were younger, you said this problem's been out for a while.
Client: It's the same thing.
Counselor: The same thing. So mostly family and now some pets.
Client: Well, I had pets then, too.
Counselor: You had pets then, too? Okay, so that's really what's bothering you here, is that you'll be away, and that's when something will happen and it'll be something bad. What about coming back? Like, you can come back?
Client: Yeah, like, I'm ready to come back, but then I'm missing home. Like, I want to go back to my family and everything's okay, but I miss, you know, where I just left because it's away from home. I know it sounds really conflicting and weird, but, you know, I like to get away. I enjoy being away from this small town.
Counselor: So, yes, you have feelings that are fighting one another.
Client: Absolutely.
Counselor: And right now, the feeling, the thought, anyway, of, you know, I would like to go on a trip is winning, but the fear thought is kind of dragging you down. So what's the sensation? Anxiety.
Client: Yeah. I get anxious. Yeah. My heart gets. Feels like it's heavy. My chest heavy. And I just. All these thoughts go through my mind, like, you know, I know my parents. Somebody can watch my pets, but they may not take care of them like I would. I don't know, it's just. I mean, you know, they've always. They'll take care of them. Client: Yeah.
Counselor:
output: Surrounding family and the pets and what might happen. So really, that's. That's it. Right. It's what might happen. It's the uncertainty.

Client: Yes, it's, there seems to be a lot that's going on and I continually don't get the help that I need, not only not from my coworker, but also my supervisor. So it just feels so that everything is my responsibility and I have to make it happen. And if I don't make it happen, it's not going to happen. And then it's just, it's all on me and I don't feel as though that it's fair. But I also don't want us to not succeed. So I don't know how to navigate those two field.
Counselor: So the weight of the work assignments is really on you. You're feeling that pressure. You want to do right by your employer and there's an emotional toll this is taken on you. Has it reached a point where you've talked to your, it's a coworker supervisor you mentioned?
Client: Yes. So I talked to my supervisor about my coworker actually assisting me with some of the projects that we have going on. And my supervisor keeps on saying, oh, they're helping out and they're doing what they're supposed to do, but they're not doing what they're supposed to do because I end up doing their work. Because, say, for example, last week we actually had to turn in this huge report that we were working on for over a month. Literally, my coworker came to me on Monday and said I didn't do my portion of the report. And I was just like, we had a month to work on a lot of time. And so I spent the next three days doing everything for their part of the report. Luckily, I had already finished my part of the report and then combined it and actually turned it into my supervisor. Of course we get the, oh, this is a wonderful, great job that you guys did. And I'm just like you guys, as.
Counselor: If you both contributed equally.
Client: Correct? Correct.
Counselor: So in three days, you made up for a month's worth of work.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So I could see how that could be. It's very stressful.
Client: Very, very taxing. Very, very taxing.
Counselor: And this wasn't an isolated incident?
Client: Oh, no. This has been going on for probably three or four months now.
Counselor: So this is almost the expectation when you get to work.
Client: Correct? Correct. I think that you hit the nail on the head. It's expected of me and nobody actually sees it as an expectation anymore.
Counselor: It's just what you do. It's just what I do. So you can know that going into work the next day, you go in, whenever that is, that there's always this probability, this chance that you could have work just thrown on you that wasn't budgeted for, you weren't planning on.
Client: Correct. And sometimes that work actually comes out from my supervisor, but it's mostly coming from my coworker. Like, I know they're not going to do their portion, so I just automatically start doing it anyway because, you know.
Counselor: You kind of have to.
Client: I know it's going to fall on my lap either today, tomorrow, next week. So I would rather be preemptive and actually start it then so that I'm not rushing like I was, like last week to finish a month's worth of work and three days worth of time. So I'm not as stressed.
Counselor: So you've tried to address this in the framework, in the context of your work. You've talked to the supervisor, to the co worker?
Client: I talked to the supervisor, I'm afraid. Well, I can't really talk to the coworker because I don't feel as though that's my position. However, I have expressed my frustration, my anger, my disappointment with my supervisor. And my supervisor keeps on saying, oh, I'll fix it, or, oh, it doesn't seem as though that they haven't done their piece of the work because I do all of it and it's turned in. So I have. But there doesn't seem to be anything happening outside of that.
Counselor: What kind of options, in terms of your job do you feel like you have now?
Client: I don't feel as though that I have any options. That's the thing. I think that either if I can, if I don't do the work and we fail, we're going to lose some of these big projects that we're working with, which then is going to impact our entire office. And if it impacts our entire office, like somebody might be let go. And because I am the newest person in our office, I feel as though that's going to be me. So I need to protect my job by doing not only my work, but my coworkers work and sometimes my supervisors work.
Counselor: So you're really figuratively fighting for survival?
Client: Correct.
Counselor: Do you think your coworker is aware that if there is a failure with getting projects done, that you would be the one that would be let go?
Client: I think, yes. I think that they understand that since they are the senior member on team, it would be most likely that the junior member myself would possibly be let go if a budget cut were to happen.
Counselor: So you're really largely stuck.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: With having to do the work.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: How about the emotions involved? You mentioned before, the frustration? Anger. Anger directed at.
Client: I think most of my anger is directed at my supervisor for not doing something because they can clearly see that something's wrong or that I'm handling a lot more, but they're not willing to step in. And I think a little bit of that anger is also at myself, because I haven't just said to my coworker, like, you need to step up and you need to do this. So I'm a little disappointed and angry at myself as well.
Counselor: You're angry at yourself, so you feel like you don't have the ability or courage to make that confrontation?
Client: I don't have the confidence to. The confidence to actually confront my coworker.
Counselor: All right, so before we dig into that too much, is it a good idea to confront the coworker?
Client: I think it would be good for them to understand how their lack of participation in our projects is impacting me and could also possibly impact our entire department. However, I don't know exactly how to say that and not come off as I'm. I know more than you, even though that you've been here longer than me.
Counselor: So you're searching for a friendly, understanding way to convey a tough subject matter.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: To someone who may or may not be receptive.
Client: Correct.
Counselor:
output: But you may presume that they're more likely to not be receptive.

And then I end up, you know, rushing right at the end of, you know, due tomorrow, and I'm getting all these five pages done. It's really hard for me.
Counselor: So you are, you are finishing the assignment on time? So the problem isn't lateness?
Client: No. I mean, I get it done.
Counselor: You get it done.
Client: It's just all at the last minute.
Counselor: So it's really the, how the time breaks out isn't working out well for you?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: You'd rather not be doing it at the last moment?
Client: No. I mean, I try not to. I mean, I set time aside to go sit down. I'm like, all right, you know, we're going to start on this paper, then sidetracked. I'm watching tv. I'm on my phone. I'm on some other website.
Counselor: So these, so these activities that you're engaging in between when you start the work and before you start writing. So, gathering the references before you start writing, you said check an email. Yeah, and other kind of. It sounds like unplanned, small activities.
Client: Yeah. I mean, there's small things that keep my attention, but that's not where my attention needs to go.
Counselor: These aren't particularly engaging activities, like something you need to do at that moment.
Client: No. I mean, I look up, you know. Right. I start on one reference, and then, oh, this article looks cool. Ooh, this article. You know, next thing I know, I'm researching octopuses or something.
Counselor: So, like, distracted.
Client: Yeah, distracted is a good word.
Counselor:
output: And then there's a moment when you kind of catch yourself and realize you haven't really started writing.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:

Client: Not expressways, but it's busy. It's busier. It's like in a mall.
Counselor: So, you know, any four lanes or six lane?
Client: Four lanes
Counselor: Yeah, four lane.
Client: So it just. It's not someplace I usually would go. And if I was gonna go, usually I would either have her go with me or my husband go with me. But she was sick, and he was at work, and so to try to.
Counselor: Understand what goes through your mind, let's try to take you back. And now you know that the prescription's there, and your daughter's sick, and I guess you don't want to ask her to drive over there.
Client: I sort of did, yeah.
Counselor: Probably not the wisest idea. So you're thinking about doing the drive, and what's going through your mind? What are the thoughts that are turning inside?
Client: I'm just, you know, I'm sort of thinking about going there, and I'm already starting to think, well, you know, what if. You know, what if I'm driving and somebody crashes into me? What if I'm driving and I can't do it? What if I just have to stop because I can't do it anymore? And it was raining, and I'm sort of like. I've got this picture of myself out in the middle of the road, you.
Counselor: Know, what's the picture look like? You're out in the middle of the.Road, and it's raining,
Client: it's stranded, and it's dark, and my, you know, my shoes are gone. I'm just like. It's like it would be a million miles to get back home.
Counselor: Pretty miserable.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: Pretty scary.
Client: Oh, terrifying.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: And I just. It's so hard to get there.
Counselor: And, Kate, as you put yourself back into that situation and have those thoughts going through your mind, what kinds of feelings go along with it? By feelings, I mean things that are inside, like, physical, like the physical anxiety. Physical things are going on.
Client: Well, fear and anxiety. And I just feel really shaky and I feel really, like, lightheaded and dizzy, and I just don't feel like I can breathe very well. And I feel like I'm gonna, like, fall over.
Counselor:
output: Is this a panic attack? Now, you told me about having some panic attacks.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: All right, Melissa, so why don't you tell me a little bit about why you're here today.
Client: I have trouble with public speaking. That's a big fear of mine.
Counselor: Okay, tell me a little bit about the feelings that are associated with your fear.
Client: I get panic attacks which affect me. I can't breathe well. I feel like I'm gonna pass out and I'm jittery. I'm just very, very anxious whenever I think about them, right before I have to do oral presentations. During them, I just feel like I'm gonna keel over. Okay.
Counselor: Where do you feel like this fear comes from? Is there an instance that occurred that caused you to be afraid or.
Client: Not really? I've always disliked it, and I've had bad experiences that probably made my fear worse, but it's. It's always been somewhat of a fear of mine since I was a child.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: It's the first time I had to try to do it.
Counselor: Okay, and what exactly is it that you're afraid of with the experience?
Client: Then I'm gonna embarrass myself by either stuttering or losing my train of thought, something along that line, so.
SPK_3: Okay.
Counselor: And if you do get embarrassed, what would that mean? How. How would that make you feel?
Client: Just stupid.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Just. Just like I couldn't do it.
Counselor: Stupid person.
Client: Yes.
SPK_3: Okay. Okay.
Counselor: Let me just ask you a little bit about that, I guess. Let me ask you first. Logically, if you made a mistake in a presentation, would that make you feel like you were always going to make mistakes in presentations to follow?
Client: Yeah, kind of. I mean, I know it's not logical, but that's how I think. I think that it's always going to happen. No matter how well prepared I am for the presentation, it's always going to go wrong somehow.
Counselor: So you would always go into it feeling like I'm going to mess up? Yes. Okay. Okay. Do you feel like it's logical to assume that just because you make a mistake, everyone's going to remember that? I mean, when someone else makes a mistake in the class, do you remember that?
Client: No. No, I don't remember it.
Counselor:
output: Okay, so then do you still feel that it's logical to think that they would remember your mistakes?
