instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Carlos. How are you feeling today?
Client: Feeling terrible. I had a wrestling match last night, and I lost my match again. I should just quit the team. I'm such a bad wrestler.
Counselor: What do you mean by again?
Client: I lost my match last week, too. I should just quit the team.
Counselor: You mean because you lost two matches, it automatically means you're going to lose your next match?
Client: Well, yes. I am clearly a bad wrestler.
Counselor: Okay, so losing is not fun. No one likes to lose. But it doesn't mean you're a bad wrestler.
Client: Yeah, I guess not. But all my other teammates won their matches. It made me feel dumb to be the only one who lost. Like I'm a terrible wrestler. I don't feel like I belong on the team anymore.
Counselor: Yes, losing is unpleasant. And those two matches weren't your best. Does that mean that you're a bad wrestler?
Client: Well, I don't know. Maybe not.
Counselor: How were you doing before you lost those two matches?
Client: We've only had four matches so far, but I won my first two matches.
Counselor: Okay, so you started off the season by winning two matches in a row, which means you do know how to wrestle. You just happened to lose two matches in a row, but that's all it was?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What else are you telling yourself about wrestling?
Client: Well, I just felt terrible after I lost those two matches, and I was thinking that if I lo. That if I lose my next match, I'm never going to be able to get a scholarship to college.
Counselor: Hold on a second, Carlos. Let me stop you right there. What if you do lose your next match? What is the worst thing that could happen? Would it be the end of the world?
Client: Um, no, I guess not. The season just started.
Counselor: How much longer do you have in the season?
Client: A few more months.
Counselor: A few more months? Which means you still have plenty of matches left. So, although losing your next match would be frustrating, you would be okay. The world would not end.
Client: Yeah, I guess you're right.
Counselor: Do you enjoy wrestling?
Client: Yes. Actually, I love wrestling. I've been wrestling since my freshman year.
Counselor: You've been wrestling for three years, and it is a sport you love participating in. Does it make sense that you said you were going to quit just a few matches into the season?
Client: No, it really doesn't.
Counselor: Are you starting to understand what you told yourself about the consequences of losing a few wrestling matches?
Client: Yes, I guess I am. I told myself that if I lost any matches this season, I'm a bad wrestler. That isn't true. Losing some of my matches doesn't automatically mean I'm a bad wrestler. It's also not the end of the world.
Counselor: Is that correct information to give yourself?
Client: No.
Counselor: Okay, I feel like you're starting to get it now. Let's look at the other things you've been telling yourself about wrestling. What else did you tell yourself?
Client: Said that if I lost any of my matches, I wouldn't get a wrestling scholarship for college.
Counselor: Is it a reasonable goal to say you're not going to lose any matches over an entire season?
Client: No, not really.
Counselor: You've lost before over the last three years, right? Have you had success in past seasons?
Client: Yes, I have. I lost a couple of matches last season, but I had a good season overall.
Counselor:
output: Okay, so you know that losing several matches throughout the course of the season isn't the end of the world. What else have you been telling yourself?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Aspen. How you doing today?
Client: I'm doing well, thank you. How about yourself?
Counselor: I'm doing all right, thanks for asking. I had met you last time for our first session, and we talked a little bit about kind of your circumstances, what brought you here. And I was hoping today we could get into trying to really figure out how we can help you. Any thoughts on your current situation? Anything changed?
Client: Nothing's really changed. I mean, I'm amazing at my job. My boss just really is someone that I hold, you know, in higher regards than others I work with especially. We went to. We went to the same college. College, of course. And he suggested I come into counseling and he's way off. Way off. So I'm just gonna, you know, let him know.
Counselor: So, as I understand it, you came into counseling because he requested it.
Client: That was what initiated it. But now it's. I need to prove him wrong.
Counselor: Alright, so at first it was because he told you it would be a good idea, but now you kind of see it as an opportunity to prove your point.
Client: Yeah, have a little bit of fun with it. Prove my point.
Counselor: What would you. What would you like to prove through this?
Client: That I'm not the one in the wrong. You know, I. I'm extremely good at my job. I mean, I am the best employee that they have ever had. Not just currently, just. I mean, just ever. I make no errors. So how can I be wrong when it comes to these circumstances with my coworkers?
Counselor: Right. So your co workers have made some criticisms about you and that led to your boss suggesting this.
Client: I would call them criticisms because it's really hard to criticize me. So I would say they take it personally that I'm better than them, you know? So I feel that it's important for me to be able to work for this particular company. It needs to be the best company. And so I need the other employees to at least be at my level. Well, I mean, that's. That's really hard for them to come to my level, but at least be above average. At least.
Counselor: All right, so you have an expectation of them to become at least close to you in terms of your skill.
Client: I mean, it's pretty hard to not make any errors when it comes to accounting with the numbers, with the amount of numbers and the volume of accounts that we have, it's hard to be as good as I am with it, as far as no errors. But yes, I expect a higher standard from the coworkers.
Counselor: And you don't feel like they're performing at that level now?
Client: No, not at all.
Counselor: And evidently you made some different comments to them which maybe they took the wrong way.
Client: I just pointed out the facts of the situation.
Counselor: What type of facts did you, when.
Client: They make mistakes and, you know, how they should be better at certain tasks. I mean, they didn't attend the same, you know, type of college as far as, you know, Ivy League as myself. However, they do have a college education so, you know, that alone would, you know, just kind of go to speak to them having some sort of ability in that area.
Counselor: So you've kind of, in a way you've expressed your disappointment with them.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: To them?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And what are some of the observations or comments they made regarding you?
Client: Oh, they told me my ego is too big, that I'm cocky. That's one. Yeah. I'm just overall, like, I don't know how you can be too confident when your ability is at that level. I mean, I am the best employee they've ever had overall. You know, I was the best student at my college. I received numerous awards from the president of the college alone. I received numerous calls from the college and other companies as well, trying to recruit me to work for them. You know, so I don't think there's, it's impossible to be overly confident, but they, you know, they consider it cocky and arrogant. Get arrogant a lot.
Counselor: The comment arrogant. So you feel they're just really, are they misunderstanding you?
Client: I think they take it as a personal attack.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Like I'm can, like I'm that concerned with them personally. Like it affect, like I'm talking about them as a person instead of just their performance at work because I'm really not concerned with them as far as like existence outside the realm of performance at work.
Counselor: Alright. So your commentary to them has nothing to do with their value as a person, more with their performance as an employee. And you feel they're misconstruing your observations about their performance?
Client: Very much so.
Counselor: They're taking it personally.
Client: Taking it personally and trying as best they can to push it back on me as I'm the one who's wrong, but I'm obviously not.
Counselor: Alright, so you're not wrong in this and you're frustrated by their reactions.
Client: I mean, I'm okay with it, you know, I mean it's, I don't really take anything they say to heart because they're not at the level to really be able to criticize me. You know, I can take criticism, you know, from constructive criticism, from someone who would, you know, be at my level or above, however, they are not. So it's really nothing. It really doesn't affect me. It does interfere with my job as far as my employer is concerned.
Counselor: Right. That's what led to you. That's what led to him recommending you come here initially. So you don't feel that they're at a level where they can really criticize you. It doesn't really bother you if they have criticism in the first place, but you can appreciate how getting along with them would be better for you as an employee.
Client: I mean. I mean, overall, I like this company. You know, I like working for it. I've been friends with my boss. I mean, we went to the same college, you know, so we have that in common. You know, he is an extraordinary person as far as his abilities, you know, I would say as in the level realm as myself. So, you know, I hold his, you know, opinion, you know, in some sort of regards above the others, so.
Counselor: Okay, so to the extent that they communicate negative sentiment to him about you, that that affects you?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And so what do you think, if anything, what do you think needs to be fixed here?
Client: Well, I think it's on their area and, you know, on their side. They didn't take what I said the wrong way.
Counselor:
output: Okay. So if they had accurately interpreted your comments, that would fix the problem?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: So, hello, Michael. Welcome back.
Client: Thank you. Hi.
Counselor: So, for this session, I'm just going to briefly discuss what we went over in our last session, including the goals that we set for you, and then we can kind of discuss how those went for you. Does that sound good?
Client: Okay,
Counselor: so what we discussed in the last session is we went over what your diet and lifestyle are like, and we discussed those goals for you, with your overall goal being to become more plant based and just healthier. And the specific goals that we set for this week were to swap out your usual breakfast of yogurt with nuts and berries for a plant based smoothie five out of seven days this week. And your second goal was to track your food intake using myfitnesspal every day this week with the goal of keeping your sugar intake to under 50 grams per day. So, starting with that first goal of swapping out your breakfast five out of seven days this week for a plant based smoothie. How did that go?
Client: I would say I had moderate success in that I had smoothies three out of, so far, six days of this week. I started the week on Sunday and now it's Friday. So a couple things that got in the way of reaching the goal. One is that I basically forgot the goal. It wasn't in the forefront of my mind. I was more focused on making smoothies for mom and not making sure I had them. And then secondly, I'm out of town from this morning until tomorrow afternoon. And so I essentially lost like a day or two mornings where I would normally be at home and be able to make a smoothie for myself. So I can try to make up for one of the smoothies tomorrow when I get home, but really need to make it more of a habit and have it in a forefront of my mind.
Counselor: So you talk a lot. You mentioned a few times that making that in the forefront of your mind. And the first thing you said was that the reason you didn't complete the goal was that you just forgot about it. So would it be alright with you if we maybe discussed some ways to increase your memory of the goal?
Client: Sure.
Counselor: All right. So what do you think you could do to remember to make this goal happen, to get up to those five smoothies?
Client: Well, a couple things. One is I have a daily, I have an app on my computer that I used to put down task items into the to do list, basically, and I review that every day. So, you know, if I have a separate diet related category for my to Dos, I could enter it there and have it there. I could put a reminder on my fridge and then also doing the meal tracking that I was doing with my fitness pal would of course make it evident that I'm not doing it. But that was a lot of work this week. I would not want to put in that much work. And then finally, I think once it gets going so it's on automatic, you're making a habit, then that in and of itself reminds me.
Counselor: So you mentioned some really good ideas. So you talked about you have this reminder app on your computer. I think that that's a great way. If it's something that you're already checking every day, then you should definitely consider adding in this reminder to make the smoothies there. And you also mentioned putting a reminder on your fridge. So insofar as continuing with this goal, if we were to rewrite it, what would you say?
Client: You mean like perhaps including items to help you reach the goal?
Counselor: Yes.
Client: And then sub to do items? In a sense, yeah. So I think that would be helpful. Listing specific actions which I'm going to take to try to help me reach this other action I'm trying to do. That would be helpful. And I think what we've talked about using my to do app is probably the best because since I go back and forth between two places during the week, I have to maintain, you know, a list of each place on the fridge. I don't necessarily pay attention to that every day. I think because I'm using my computer every day and I use this to do that every day. That's a natural place to start.
Counselor:
output: Okay, so I'm just going to write it down so I can send it to you in an email what our modified version of the smooth equal will be. So what you were saying was would you like to maintain the five out of seven days or would you like to increase it or decrease it?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hey, Carly. How are you doing today?
Client: I'm good. How are you?
Counselor: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. What's been going on this last week?
Client: I've just been feeling kind of in a rut. I mean, I've been looking for a job and haven't really gotten anywhere. And then I had a drink the other night, and I just felt like me not having a job and me going out and having that drink, it wasn't deserved. And I just felt like such a loser because that was the time that I should have been at work if I had a job, and instead I was at the bar drinking. So I had one drink, and then it led to another. Cause then I just felt worse and I figured I had one, so.
Counselor: All right, so how much did you drink in total?
Client: I think I lost track after four or five.
Counselor: How long had it been since you had a drink before that?
Client: I did really well. It was, I think, like three weeks.
Counselor: Three weeks?
Client: Three weeks or so.
Counselor: Oh, so you did really well and then you had one drink and that just made you feel like you weren't successful?
Client: I felt like a loser.
Counselor: Felt like a loser. And you feel that kind of led to drinking some more? So you had a rough time with things?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. How about now?
Client: I mean, now I just kind of. I don't know, I'm afraid to go back. Like, I'm afraid to go out with, like, some friends. They invite me out to dinner, but I know there's alcohol and.
Counselor: Is that where you were when you had that first drink? Was that with friends?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right, so there's a few things going on. We've talked in the past, right, about separating the behavior from the person. Right. So behavior is what we do, not who we are. You remember those discussions? And correct me if I'm wrong, but it sounds like I'm going to use some different words than you used. But it sounds like when you had that first drink, you're kind of ashamed that you had a drink and you had it during the time when you would have been working.
Client: Yeah, that's pretty accurate.
Counselor: That's pretty accurate. So, taking yourself back to that moment, right. We had that first. That first drink, like, you finished that first drink. What was your thought at that moment?
Client: Just, like, shameful. Like, I did really, really well, and then here I was, and I had just finished a drink, and I knew I wanted another one.
Counselor: Okay, so shameful is kind of like the feeling, but the thought is I did really, really well. Right. So that's what you're thinking was, I did really, really well. And what was that the end of the thought? Or was that. Was there more before you had that next drink?
Client: I guess just I was doing well, and then I had a drink, and I just felt like an awful person. So figured what was the. The hurt and having more.
Counselor: So the sequence would have been you had the drink, you felt shameful. At the same time, you're thinking that you were doing really well, and then just really, as you said before, you just felt like a loser. And then you decided, might as well just have the second drink. So another thought might be that, like, I might as well, just might as well just have a second drink.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. So you can see how there's some thoughts and some feelings at work. Right. As you finished that first drink, was it fairly quick? Were those thoughts and feelings fairly occur fairly quickly after the drink?
Client: Yeah, I would say as I was finishing and then finished.
Counselor: Right away, you regretted it. And in that regret, as you thought about it, thought, might as well just continue drinking now because you kind of blew it.
Client: Yeah, I already messed up. I might as well keep going.
Counselor: Okay. And that's a common cycle to fall into. And you had three weeks where you hadn't had a drink prior to that. So let's look at this. Let's try to separate the behavior from the self a little bit. If you had a friend who was in the same predicament, who had a history of using alcohol and then had three weeks without any alcohol use, and then their behavior was to have a drink, what would you think of them?
Client: I would think that they had a rough day or something must have happened where? I mean, it's just one drink.
Counselor: Okay. They had a rough day. One drink. And what would you think of their behavior? How would you categorize that behavior?
Client: I guess just they made a mistake.
Counselor: So not ideal, depending on their point of view. Maybe a little irresponsible.
Client: Yeah, I think irresponsible would be irresponsible.
Counselor: But you wouldn't necessarily characterize them as a bad person. No, but their behavior was a bit irresponsible, you know, in terms of, like, the recovery plan, which would be to not drink. But when you apply that same examination to your own situation, how do you characterize yourself after you had that first drink?
Client: It was my mistake. It was in it. It makes me a worse person for doing it.
Counselor:
output: So you see how you're being a little. Well, it'd be quite a bit rougher on yourself. Like, your evaluation of yourself is. Is fairly harsh. You mentioned loser earlier and ashamed. Whereas you wouldn't necessarily evaluate someone else that way. How would you evaluate your behavior? How would you judge your behavior of taking that first drink?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:

Counselor: Any expressways or bridges to get there?
Client: Not expressways, but it's busy. It's busier. It's like in a mall.
Counselor: So, you know, any four lanes or six lane?
Client: Four lanes
Counselor: Yeah, four lane.
Client: So it just. It's not someplace I usually would go. And if I was gonna go, usually I would either have her go with me or my husband go with me. But she was sick, and he was at work, and so to try to.
Counselor: Understand what goes through your mind, let's try to take you back. And now you know that the prescription's there, and your daughter's sick, and I guess you don't want to ask her to drive over there.
Client: I sort of did, yeah.
Counselor: Probably not the wisest idea. So you're thinking about doing the drive, and what's going through your mind? What are the thoughts that are turning inside?
Client: I'm just, you know, I'm sort of thinking about going there, and I'm already starting to think, well, you know, what if. You know, what if I'm driving and somebody crashes into me? What if I'm driving and I can't do it? What if I just have to stop because I can't do it anymore? And it was raining, and I'm sort of like. I've got this picture of myself out in the middle of the road, you.
Counselor: Know, what's the picture look like? You're out in the middle of the.Road, and it's raining,
Client: it's stranded, and it's dark, and my, you know, my shoes are gone. I'm just like. It's like it would be a million miles to get back home.
Counselor: Pretty miserable.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: Pretty scary.
Client: Oh, terrifying.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Tony, you've been given this diagnosis of schizophrenia by one of your doctors. I just wondered what it's like for you and what the main problems are.
Client: The main problem is these. Well, they tell me that it's a problem to do with musketsophrenia. These voices, they come and they. I heard these people talking about me and talking about how rubbish I am and what a failure I am, and I really just wish they'd leave me alone.
Counselor: Yes, that's extremely negative content to what's being said. So it's a clear voice outside of your head, is it?
Client: Yeah, yeah, it's two voices. And, you know, sometimes they're talking to me and sometimes they're talking about me, but it's always really negative. There's no helpful things there at all.
Counselor: It sounds like these voices are associated with a feeling of sadness. Am I getting that right or is that another feeling?
Client: Oh, well, when I let them, they get me really down. They get me really, really down. But, you know, I'm fighting these. Fighting them still, you know.
Counselor: What are you doing to fight?
Client: Well, there's where I get into a real problem, because I shout back at them. And, you know, my neighbors, they. Well, you know, they don't understand and they say they don't hear these voices. Sometimes I wonder if my neighbors are in on it as well, but, you know, they say that they can't hear them, but I don't understand how they can't hear them because they're so loud.
Counselor: So loud.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What do you make of these voices, then? Do you think it's part of an illness, or do you think the neighbors are doing it? Or what do you think?
Client: Well, you know, I think there was somebody once that I really didn't get on with at school, and I think it's him. And I think he's kind of got these people to be kind of harassing me. I think they're trying to drive me mad, I think, is what they're trying to do.
Counselor: That's a very distressing experience. I can understand that. So do you think other people can hear them if they're very loud?
Client: Well, you know what? They say they can't, but that makes me wonder if they know what they're. If maybe they're on it. But everybody says that they can't. And, you know, I don't know. I've tried my CPN said, you know, why don't I put a recorder on, you know, when the voices are there and, you know, it didn't pick them up, but I don't know. Maybe it was faulty or something. It just nobody else can hear them, I guess, is the answer to your question. Or everybody says they can't.
Counselor: Even with the tape recorder, you still don't think. Well, you think other people maybe can see them, hear them?
Client: Well, sometimes I think people can hear them, and sometimes I think, you know, well, maybe my CPN's right. Maybe it's my imagination.
Counselor: So is it just you that hears voices, or do other people in society hear voices, Tony?
Client: Well, there's somebody else at the day center, and he hears voices that other people can't hear. And we've talked together, and I can't hear the voices that he's hearing.
Counselor:
output: That's interesting, isn't it?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Well, Meredith, we know each other, but the way we usually start a CBT session is to set an agenda. So we might have several ideas about what we want on the agenda. But the first thing is usually for us to make a problem list together about whatever it is that you might want to work on.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: And then we'll do the problem list, and then we'll explain, explore the thoughts and the behaviors that might be related to the problem. And hopefully, by the end of our time together, we'll have a clearer idea about what's causing the problem and some ideas about how to maybe change things.
Client: Sounds good.
Counselor: All right.
Client: So one thing that I've been noticing lately is that I have a tendency to kind of hang back in groups, and I tend to observe instead of participate.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: And a lot of times I get really nervous when I feel like I'm expected to speak up. And I want to speak up, but I kind of feel like I freeze.
Counselor: Okay. And so in particular, then, in groups, the setting is big groups, little groups. Does it matter?
Client: It doesn't matter a whole lot, but generally, I guess medium size. Like, you know, in classes that I have usually, like maybe twelve people or so. So relatively small, medium. I don't know what size that is.
Counselor: Okay. And so. But in your head, you probably would say, I would like to speak up, but for some reason, you feel inside some anxiety or nervousness about that.
Client: Definitely.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: And then sometimes when I try to force myself to speak up, when I actually don't feel ready, I get like. I feel like my throat's closing and I get a red face.
Counselor: Okay. All right. So that's sort of one possible issue for us to talk about. Could you maybe give me a specific example of a particular group situation, as recent as you can, where you had this feeling of hanging back and maybe. Maybe some fear of evaluation?
Client: So in my statistics class each week, we have a. It's called an inclusion activity. And generally, I guess it's supposed to help people feel like the group's more cohesive and included, but I usually experience it as the opposite. So there's usually a task at the beginning of each class of like, take off your shoe and talk. Talk about the most interesting place your shoe has been. Stuff like this in stats that, um, usually I get really nervous and I feel like I can't think of anything to say. And I feel like I usually end up saying something really awkward or lame, and I just don't feel good about it. Like, I feel.
Counselor: Yeah. Can you give me that specific example of the recent time when maybe. And then. And what you said, too, including sort of the beginning, what happened and then how it ended.
Client: Yeah. So when we did this activity, it's, like, a really weird example. When we did this activity, you know, probably six or seven people had gone in front of me, and I was, like, not listening to anything that anyone else was saying, just totally self absorbed in terms of, like, oh, God, what am I going to say? And not being able to think of anything. And then when it was my turn, I was wearing a pair of shoes that, like, are kind of, like, they have lace on them. And so I took it off and I said, I like these shoes because I get cool tan lines from them. So I didn't even really answer the question that was like, where have these shoes been? Or, like, the coolest place these shoes have been? Or something like that. And then after I went, I didn't really listen to anything else anyone said because I was still, like, stuck on, why didn't I answer the question and just kind of feeling awkward.
Counselor: Okay, so what I'm doing here is I've got several columns that I'm building, and the first one is, you're in the stats class, and you're going through an inclusion activity. And the second one is the thoughts that you're having. What thoughts are going through your mind? And the thoughts are, oh, God, what am I going to say? Those are the early thoughts. And then maybe the later thoughts are, why didn't I even answer the question?
Client: Yeah. And, like, why can't I ever be articulate?
Counselor: Okay. Why can't I ever be articulate? Okay. And then our third column are the emotions that you might be feeling. And so as you're in that situation and people are taking their turn, the teacher says, you're doing the inclusion activity. People are taking their turns. And what are you feeling? How would you describe your emotional state?
Client: Nervous. Yeah. Like, fearful. And, like, it's almost like I'm anticipating. Anticipating embarrassment.
Counselor: Mm hmm.
Client: So I don't know that's a feeling or not, but usually I feel embarrassed.
Counselor: I put that in the thought okay. Column just because it seems like the anticipation of it is probably a thought, but embarrassment when you're in the middle of it is probably a fear. Does that make sense? And then. So I got nervous, fearful, embarrassed as the emotions, and on a scale of zero, not at all. 100 being the most of that feeling you could ever have, how would you rate? Let's get rid of nervous because it's sort of covered by fearful. How would you rate fearful. And how would you rate embarrassed?
Client: Maybe fearful? Like a four. Okay, four or five. I don't know.
Counselor: Four out of five.
Client: Out of 140.
Counselor:
output: Okay. I was gonna say. Oh, feeling pretty calm. So a 40 or a 50?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Zoe, how you doing today?
Client: I'm good, how are you?
Counselor: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. I know that the last time we spoke, we talked about spending today's session working on units of distress. These different levels, different exercises that cause increasingly more stress around the specific phobia you have. And I know you mentioned it related to a dog, but I didn't get a lot of information last time about how that kind of all formed. So I was hoping we could start there with what happened that made you afraid of this dog.
Client: Sure, sure.
Counselor: Tell me about that.
Client: Okay, so I've had an issue that started about when I was a little bit younger. When I was about ten years old, I was really active. I was playing outside all the time. And my neighbors had large dogs that were always in their yard. They would always be outside running around, and we were separated by a fence. And if I was playing outside or like kicking a ball around or doing anything with a friend, and I had to go after the ball, it would be near the fence. And especially if I wasn't looking, I would be leaning down to grab the ball or just have my back turned. And they would come up, they would be really excited, and they would jump on the fence, and I never would be expecting it, and they would always startle me, and I would always feel this sense of fear and uneasiness around them. And so I've kind of always been a little bit more uncomfortable around dogs since all of that happened.
Counselor: And how old were you?
Client: I was about ten.
Counselor: Oh, you mentioned that. Yeah, you're around ten. And they would startle you. Would you like, jump?
Client: Yeah, yeah. It was like a whole body reaction, I guess, because I wouldn't ever be looking, I wouldn't know that they were coming, and then they would just be up against the fence, like barking and jumping, and I felt like they were gonna jump over and try to get me.
Counselor: And since that time, you haven't been a big fan of dogs?
Client: No, not really.
Counselor: And for this exercise specifically, there was one dog in particular that you wanted to kind of work through that fear?
Client: Yeah. Yeah. Cause there was an incident that happened more recently at my friend's house, and it was a really big problem. I was at a party last weekend, and they had a bunch of people outside. The dog was out loose, and it's there, and so it's never really a problem. It's always kind of around. Doesn't really come near me. I can always just kind of keep my distance from it. But we were outside, and they were playing with it, and I wasn't really paying attention. And they're throwing the frisbee for the dog between each other, and the dog was facing me, and I turned around, and it was running towards me, and I didn't realize it, and I just saw him coming up at me, just kind of like how the dogs had when I was a kid, and it really was unexpected, and it startled me, and I kind of thought, like, I did, like, when I was a kid, like, they were gonna come get me, even though he didn't. He didn't come near me. And it was a really big problem for me because I was all shaken up, and I tried to go inside and calm myself down, and I couldn't, and I had to leave. I had to leave the house, and I've been really uncomfortable ever since.
Counselor: So this is particularly stressful, this particular dog. What kind of dog is it?
Client: It was a full grown german shepherd. Yeah. His name. His name is Thor.
Counselor: His name is Thor?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you want to be able to interact specifically with Thor. You want to conquer that fear.
Client: Yeah, because I've been really hesitant to go back over there because her family, it's my good friend, so her family's super nice. And they said, like, you know, we'll lock the dog up. Like, you can. Can still come over, but I would just feel really guilty because it's their house and I'm over there. Well, I used to be over there all the time, and now if I go over there, that means that they have to keep the dog, like, away or, you know, not really where I can, like, be near it, because I'm gonna have that. That fear.
Counselor: All right, so it's important for you to get over the specific fear, and the owners of the dog you think will cooperate with the exercise that we have here?
Client: Yeah, yeah. They're so nice. So definitely, if I said, like, can you help me with this? They would totally be involved with me.
Counselor: All right, so you're getting started developing these units of distress over three days. I just want to establish the scale before we get started. Okay. One to ten. One is, like, really mild level of distress, and ten is, like, when you're in person with that dog, he's just stand there with you. So ten would be a lot of stress, the kind of anxiety and panic you described earlier. And one would be. It registers on the scale, but it's really minor. It doesn't bother you that much. So I'm going to list these different exposures, these different activities, and if you can rate them from one to ten.
Client: Okay. Okay, I understand.
Counselor: Does that make sense?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So we're going to build like a hierarchy of these different levels of distress.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Now, if there's any of these activities that or exposures that you just don't want to have any part of, just say that that's okay.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: All right. But if you think there's something that you could tolerate at some point, let's go ahead and put them on the scale and rate them. We can always take them off later.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: If you think of any others, mention them and I can add them to this list.
Client: Okay, perfect.
Counselor:
output: So I'm going to start with what I believe is the lower levels of distress, like the activities that are associated with lower levels of distress for you and this dog, like, for you and your reaction with this dog. But I may be out of order. Really? My educated guesses. So don't feel like you have to increment the scale for each one that I read. Okay. It doesn't have to be the first one's one, the next one's two. I might have some that go backwards or that don't register at all.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Carly. How you doing today?
Client: Doing okay.
Counselor: You doing okay?
Client: I guess, yeah.
Counselor: Not sure.
Client: I don't know, just the same.
Counselor: Yeah, still a little down.
Client: Yeah, I've been sleeping a lot. Going to work is a struggle. I don't really ever want to go. Just I haven't been eating much, so I think I've lost like ten pounds since past, like four months or so.
Counselor: Past four months?
Client: Um, just the guy. I don't know, I just haven't really been doing anything.
Counselor: You still been working?
Client: Well, yeah, yeah.
Counselor: But not much else?
Client: No, I usually just go to work and go home.
Counselor: Tell me what happens after you arrive at home, like after work?
Client: Um, well, my fiance tries to talk to me and really I just kind of want to go to sleep for just. I don't know. I tried, I tried reading the other day. Cause I used to like that and it's just, I think I got like into two pages and put the book down and decided to go to bed.
Counselor: What were you thinking when you put the book down?
Client: Just that I wasn't really happy doing it. I didn't really get any enjoyment out of it.
Counselor: I. And before you were depressed, which is, I guess about eight months now, you did enjoy reading?
Client: Mm hmm. Oh, yeah, all the time.
Counselor: So what would you have thought if you had to put a book down back then?
Client: Oh, I used to fall asleep reading. I would be up till like two in the morning just reading a book.
Counselor: Something you look forward to?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But not now?
Client: No, I just didn't really get any. I just wanted to try it and then I put it back down and was like.
Counselor: Were there other things that you used to enjoy doing that you don't feel motivated or comfortable to do now?
Client: Yeah, I used to be a runner and then I tried going for a run the other morning with my dog and I. I think we walked a block and that was pretty much it. I just couldn't wait for it to be over.
Counselor: Alright, so it wasn't a pleasant experience. Was there any part of it you connected with when you were running, like when you first started?
Client: Not really. I mean, it was a change to be outdoors and I realized I hadn't really seen the sun in a while, so. But other than that, I just, I had the intention of going out to run. I had my running shoes on and my dog was really excited. And then by the time I got out there, I was like, yeah, we're gonna walk. And then I thought about walking like our normal route. And by the time I got to the corner, I was like, yeah, we're gonna turn around and walk back.
Counselor: So what was the feeling like when you returned to your home after planning to run and then kind of walking and coming back?
Client: Kind of a mix of, like, relief just because it was over, and then, I guess more sadness because I didn't do anything. I didn't do what I had intended to do.
Counselor: Sadness, maybe disappointment.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So I've seen you a few times now, and based on those conversations, and, of course, what you said today, it seems like you have, for a variety of reasons, given up on the activities that you used to enjoy, you're not motivated toward them anymore.
Client: Yeah, I guess you could say that.
Counselor: And that's a common symptom of depression. I think we've talked about this a little bit before. So it's tough when you're depressed to find joy, satisfaction, happiness in activities that you once enjoyed. So we've been working with the cognitive piece. Right, like we did last time, we talked about the automatic thoughts that come up and kind of how that leads to some of the feelings of sadness and what we can do with the self talk. I'd like to talk about a different technique today that approaches the problem from a different angle. We'll continue to work the cognitive angle, but I want to add a new angle. And the technique is called behavioral activation. The theory behind it is that if you engage, if you schedule and engage in activities that you once enjoyed, even if you kind of have to fight your way through it a little bit, like with the running, that will connect to your mood. Right. Remember, we believe in cognitive therapy, that affect and behavior and cognition are all connected. So what you're thinking affects your behavior and your mood and what you do. Your behavior affects your thinking and your mood. Does that kind of make sense based on what we talked about?
Client: It does, yeah.
Counselor: So you mentioned the reading was one thing you like to do. That's tough to do. Now you try unsuccessfully with the reading and I the running. Anything else you could think of that maybe we could plan for you to do, even if it's just a short time, even if it's a little bit uncomfortable, that we could plan to do? That would be an activity that you used to enjoy?
Client: Well, my fiance and I used to go out with two other couples, and we used to go out once or twice a week, and even if it's just each other's houses, but we haven't really seen them in a while. They've tried to schedule things, but I've kind of come up with reasons of not feeling well or to kind of just stay home.
Counselor: So they're trying to initiate meeting, going out, doing something, and you're. You're kind of pushing them off.
Client: Yeah, I just. I haven't really wanted to see anybody lately.
Counselor:
output: All right, so that's. So we have reading, running, and then going out with these two other couples. Anything else you can think of that you used to really enjoy before that you can't quite motivate yourself to do now?

Counselor: Hello, Kathy. How you doing today? You okay? I know when you spoke last time, you had some goals that you want to talk about this time. Are you ready to do that?
Client: I need to. Yeah?
Counselor: Yeah. What do you have in mind?
Client: I just keep thinking about, you know, losing this weight, and I just. I really want to do it, and I just. I just can't get there, and I don't know why I.
Counselor: So you're frustrated.
Client: So ridiculous.
Counselor: Yeah, frustrated trying to lose the weight. Now, you'd said before that you had a specific number of pounds in mind, a specific amount of weight to lose. Do you still have that in mind?
Client: I would like 20 pounds.
Counselor: 20 pounds.
Client: I mean, I would like more, but I've tried to do more in the past, and I don't even get past a couple of days, so if I can do 20, that would be great.
Counselor: All right. And you tried before, and what do you think got in the way?
Client: I don't know. I guess it wasn't convenient. You know, I want to do it, and it means a lot, you know, for me and my family. I think I'd be a lot healthier.
Counselor: It's important to you. Yeah.
Client: But just, like, something always gets in the way, you know? And then I lose focus. I'm not very good at staying focused on stuff like that anyway, so.
Counselor: All right, so loss of focus. So you start trying to lose the weight, and your focus gets disrupted, and I forget.
Client: And then I make, you know, spaghetti casserole for six people, and then I eat a lot of it, and that's carbs and cheese and fat. And then I will eat what my kids don't eat. And then it's just like, I forget that I'm supposed to be making healthy choices.
Counselor: All right, so you know how to lose weight, and you know, you can lose weight, but your focus is a little off when you're, when you're trying, and that's. That's causing the problem.
Client: I think so, yeah.
Counselor: Could we break that goal of losing 20 pounds down into smaller units, like, say, five pounds, do you think?
Client: Well, maybe, yeah. Cause I've never. I always just keep, like, the chunk of weight, you know, ahead of me. I don't break it into smaller increments. That might work. I mean, I don't know how. I'd have to stay on top of it, though. Weigh myself every day.
Counselor: Is that something you can do.
Client: I'm so busy. I don't know.
Counselor: Or once a week.
Client: I probably do once a week. Put a sticky note somewhere or something, you know, maybe. Yeah. I mean, I want to try. I'm going to say yes because I want to try it, you know?
Counselor: So you mentioned the loss of focus is one problem. How about motivation? Do you feel motivated to move through all those steps, like five pounds and five pounds and so on.
Client: Right now? Yes. I think I would need a. Something to keep me going, you know.
Counselor: Week to week, a little bit of that. Something extra to help you stay motivated.
Client: Yeah. Like when you're. Sometimes when, you know, your kid does your homework early or does their homework early, and you can give them a special treat for dessert that helps, you know, keep it going.
Counselor: Okay. So some sort of activity or item that you enjoy that you could reserve for when you reach that goal of, say, the first five pounds.
Client: Right, right. I would love. I mean, I'm just. I've been so embarrassed, you know, lately. So I feel like I just. If I can find something that keeps me bone at me, keeps you motivated, that would be great.
Counselor: All right. Do you have an activity or item in mind that we could put in place as something you could reward yourself.
Client: With, like, after the first five pounds?
Counselor: Well, there's a few ways we could do it. We could do that. So you reach five pounds, and then you can give yourself that reward. Or it could be for something you do every day. If that day you're successful in eating the way you want to eat, what do you think would benefit you more?
Client: Maybe something every day. So I remember, you know, I just get so distracted by other stuff. So there was something every day that maybe I put out, almost like a goal at the end of the day or something.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: You know, if I made the right choices.
Counselor: Yes. So, you know, each and every day, as you're trying to lose weight, you're aware when that day comes to a close, if you had a successful day or a less than successful day.
Client: Right.
Counselor: And if you have a successful day, then you could engage in an activity or receive an item that we work out in advance that, you know, would motivate you.
Client: Right. And that could be, you know, maybe watching, like, a favorite tv show.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: You know, because I don't watch tv at night because I'm so busy, you know, cleaning up and everything. And maybe I could just take some time for myself because I did something good, you know, and just watch a tv show.
Counselor: All right, so let's do that on a day you know, towards the evening when, you know, you have had a successful day. By what time would you know in the evening?
Client: Probably as I'm preparing dinner. If I prepare a good dinner, or if I prepare fun food for my kids, but I don't eat it, like, chicken nuggets and french fries and stuff, I would know, you know, maybe by, like, six or seven. Okay.
Counselor:
output: Say seven.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: So, hello, Michael. Welcome back.
Client: Thank you. Hi.
Counselor: So, for this session, I'm just going to briefly discuss what we went over in our last session, including the goals that we set for you, and then we can kind of discuss how those went for you. Does that sound good?
Client: Okay,
Counselor: so what we discussed in the last session is we went over what your diet and lifestyle are like, and we discussed those goals for you, with your overall goal being to become more plant based and just healthier. And the specific goals that we set for this week were to swap out your usual breakfast of yogurt with nuts and berries for a plant based smoothie five out of seven days this week. And your second goal was to track your food intake using myfitnesspal every day this week with the goal of keeping your sugar intake to under 50 grams per day. So, starting with that first goal of swapping out your breakfast five out of seven days this week for a plant based smoothie. How did that go?
Client: I would say I had moderate success in that I had smoothies three out of, so far, six days of this week. I started the week on Sunday and now it's Friday. So a couple things that got in the way of reaching the goal. One is that I basically forgot the goal. It wasn't in the forefront of my mind. I was more focused on making smoothies for mom and not making sure I had them. And then secondly, I'm out of town from this morning until tomorrow afternoon. And so I essentially lost like a day or two mornings where I would normally be at home and be able to make a smoothie for myself. So I can try to make up for one of the smoothies tomorrow when I get home, but really need to make it more of a habit and have it in a forefront of my mind.
Counselor: So you talk a lot. You mentioned a few times that making that in the forefront of your mind. And the first thing you said was that the reason you didn't complete the goal was that you just forgot about it. So would it be alright with you if we maybe discussed some ways to increase your memory of the goal?
Client: Sure.
Counselor: All right. So what do you think you could do to remember to make this goal happen, to get up to those five smoothies?
Client: Well, a couple things. One is I have a daily, I have an app on my computer that I used to put down task items into the to do list, basically, and I review that every day. So, you know, if I have a separate diet related category for my to Dos, I could enter it there and have it there. I could put a reminder on my fridge and then also doing the meal tracking that I was doing with my fitness pal would of course make it evident that I'm not doing it. But that was a lot of work this week. I would not want to put in that much work. And then finally, I think once it gets going so it's on automatic, you're making a habit, then that in and of itself reminds me.
Counselor: So you mentioned some really good ideas. So you talked about you have this reminder app on your computer. I think that that's a great way. If it's something that you're already checking every day, then you should definitely consider adding in this reminder to make the smoothies there. And you also mentioned putting a reminder on your fridge. So insofar as continuing with this goal, if we were to rewrite it, what would you say?
Client: You mean like perhaps including items to help you reach the goal?
Counselor:
output: Yes.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Rebecca. How you doing today?
Client: I'm doing okay.
Counselor: Doing okay?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What's been going on?
Client: Well, nothing too bad. I kind of got in a little bit of a. Like, a fender bender accident.
Counselor: A car accident?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What happened?
Client: Well, we were at a stop sign, and I was, like, actually a red light, and there was one car here, another car here, and then I was here, and the car was behind, coming up behind me, and then they hit me, and then I hit the car in front of me.
Counselor: Oh, yeah? You okay?
Client: I kind of, you know, you know.
Counselor: Just the usual rock back and forth.
Client: Yeah, yeah.
Counselor: But other than that, you're okay? No, I got a couple, you know.
Client: Little bruises from, like, hitting the steering wheel. I'm like, yeah, but I'm. I'm okay. My body's okay.
Counselor: So, physically, you feel okay?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Were you, like, checked out by your physician or anything?
Client: Yeah, everything's okay here. I didn't break anything or pull anything.
Counselor: How about emotionally?
Client: It's been kind of hard to, like, be, like, get in my car again afterwards. Like, I've been still been going to work and everything, but, like, I realized last night, like, my boyfriend was like, oh, do you want to go on a trip this weekend? And I was kind of, like, maybe not. Like, I'm kind of, like, hesitant to get back in the car.
Counselor: So when he said that about the trip, what was the thought that came in your mind?
Client: I'm gonna get hurt.
Counselor:
output: So it was really all about the car?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Miss Payne. My name is Rebecca, and I will be your therapist today. And I see on your notes that you prefer to be called Kelly. Is that correct?
Client: Yes, ma'am. My name is Kelly, but a lot of people call me Kelly Joe. They do? Yeah. My papa in particular. He likes to call me Joe. Kelly Joe. I was named after my great grandfathers.
Counselor: Okay, well, would you prefer that I call you Kelly or Kelly Joe?
Client: No, just call me Kelly. I think Kelly Joe is really country. Okay, we'll just go with Kelly.
Counselor: All right, Kelly. The first thing I want to do is I'm going to explain our roles that we have today in our session. And of course, you know, as I said, I'm your therapist, but you're also actively participating in this session. And anytime you have a question, if you have any comments, if you don't understand something, I want you to tell me so that I can make sure that you understand everything that we're doing, that we're talking about, and it will be actively. Yeah. Between both of us will be a team, if you want.
Client: Oh, I definitely ask questions. Trust me. I like to ask a lot of questions. I like to talk.
Counselor: Well, that's good. And then the other thing, we have an agenda that I'm going to try to stick by. We want to start off with a mood check. I'll just kind of see how you're feeling today. We'll talk about your presenting problems, and we'll go into making some goals, and I'll explain a little bit of the theory that I use for our sessions. Kind of do a little educational piece to make sure you understand what's going on, and we'll give a summary. And also, I may have some homework that we can talk about.
Client: Okay. Because I sure do have lots of problems. I can tell you about tons of problems.
Counselor:
output: Yeah.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, mister Urban. It's nice to see you again. From our previous session, I know you spoke about the relationship you and your wife were going through. In the bad terms, she got left off. So I want to ask you, what would make you cheat on your wife?
Client: You know, I've been asked that question every day for the past two, three weeks. And the only thing I can respond with is what would make a wife cheat on her husband? I mean, it's petty. I know it's petty. But I loved her. And finding out that more than once she was with somebody else, that took something from me that I couldn't get back. And for months I was dealing with. What could I have done? What was it? What did I do? Because it has to have been me. She's too nice a person for that, right? She's too smart a person for that, right? And then weeks of me finally understanding that it wasn't me. A decision that you make is a decision that you make. So when Susie, my administrative assistant, came into the picture, I had a decision that I had to make. I have to take it off and spend time with Susie. Or keep it on and spend many a night alone. So why? You figure it out.
Counselor: So do you think that you did it for revenge? Were you trying to get back at your wife?
Client: I guess. I mean, what else could it be? Yeah, maybe I am that petty. But it's just. It's not love anymore.
Counselor: So why are you still in a marriage, mister Urban? If it's not love, if it's not for love, why do you feel that you must stay in America?
Client: Because that's the type of household I was brought up in.
Counselor: Explain that to me.
Client: My dad always told me that you take care of your business and your girl is your business. You never leave her. You take care of her no matter what. That's what you do. So when I got older, I asked him, what do you mean you never leave her? He said, divorce is not an option. That's pretty much how it is in my household.
Counselor: So are you saying because of how you were raised up is why you're still in the marriage?
Client: It's the only thing that makes sense.
Counselor: Are you happy?
Client: Do I seem happy?
Counselor: Have you spoken to your wife about this?
Client: No. So everything that I feel, everything that I am is stuck on the inside. This is actually the first time I've actually talked about any of her.
Counselor: Okay, mister Ermen, so let's try this exercise. I'm gonna pull out chairs, so pretend that that this is your wife here. Why are we here and express your feelings.
Client: Why do I have to do this?
Counselor: Because you never spoke about it. Right? So express your feelings. Let it out, and see how you would tell her what you're feeling inside. Do you feel uncomfortable?
Client: I felt uncomfortable since the moment I found out that you just didn't love me anymore. I felt uncomfortable every single night I've been in the guest room because I just couldn't take being with you. I felt uncomfortable since the very moment I felt like it was okay because of what you did to me. To take off my wedding band, to forget my vows, to forget you, to try and be something that I'm not. Every night that I was with Susie, I imagined that I was with you, but not who you are now. I imagine that I was with the woman that I first met, woman that I first loved. But you're not the same person anymore. I haven't been the same person over a year. Every day that I wake up and I see your face, I have to imagine that you are that same person because that's the. The only thing that keeps me around. That and the fact that I just don't think I can make. And it's not because I love you so much anymore, because it's not you that I love. It's not because of anything religious. It's because I don't want to deal with my family.
Counselor: I know that was hard to do. Mister Urban, are you doing all right? Are you feeling okay?
Client: I'm fine.
Counselor: Okay. So I want you to realize, like, can you not see that your belief is causing this pain inside your depression and your unhappiness?
Client: It makes sense, if that's what you're saying. The question is, how am I supposed to deal with, like, right now? I know I've got the option of staying with her and dealing with this every day for as long as I stay with her and deal with this or just leaving, and then I have to deal with everything else around me. How am I supposed to get past that? That's my question. And I don't know. I don't even know if that's really the right way to go.
Counselor: What is everything else?
Client: My family, the judgments. What? I'm gonna have to deal with my brother, who, by the way, is married, and he's not dealing with infidelity, but he's dealing with the same depression I am. The love isn't there anymore. We don't get divorced. Not in my household.
Counselor: So would you rather satisfy what, your family standard? Rather to be happy? Is that what you're saying?
Client: Sounds like it.
Counselor: Have you spoken to your family about this?
Client: No.
Counselor:
output: And what do you think they would say if they were to find out.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Do you have on your presentation, do you have so many bullet points you want to cover?

Counselor: Okay. Would it help to time the deep breathing with reviewing each one of those bullet points?
Client: I never thought about that.
Counselor: I don't know how many bullet points you'd have in a presentation. Maybe you'd have ten or 20, something like that. Yeah, depending on how long it is. So maybe you, as you start to review a certain bullet point, as you're trying to get it into your memory and think about it, you breathe in really deeply. And then as you continue on, you just let out that breath really slowly.
Client: Like a rhythm, sort of. Yeah, I can.
Counselor: And then you go to the next bullet point and do the same thing.

Counselor: I'm just thinking it'd be some way to structure so you would get in so many breaths.
Client: So I wouldn't forget. Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. Something that kind of becomes a habit.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Just make sure you keep your bullet points at a length, not a few paragraphs, but just a few seconds each, so you can get a good deep breath. Or you could, you know, if you did have a longer bullet point, you could have, obviously several breaths, but just some rhythm that you could kind of grab onto something concrete.

Counselor: Because I know that in that moment, things are probably, like you mentioned, zoning out and it becomes very easy to lose your anchors.
