instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Elizabeth. How you doing today?
Client: I'm all right.
Counselor: How things been going since the last time I met?
Client: It's about the same. I'm still feeling pretty down. I mean, I just. I feel really stuck and not happy, and I just don't know why.
Counselor: Okay, so there's a few things going on there. You said you're feeling stuck, not happy, and sound like you're a little confused as to what's going on, what's causing it. Do you have any suspicions about what might be causing it?
Client: I mean, I've been feeling, like, really isolated lately, you know, because I'm a stay at home mom. It's hard. There's not a lot of people, you know, right at my fingertips to spend my time with, you know, obviously my family, but. So I guess, you know, I kind of. I had some friends in the neighborhood, but, like, our friendships just kind of fizzled out, and I. Ever since then, it's just like, I don't really feel like doing much. I just kind of feel like, what's the point? And let my husband take care of a lot of stuff. You know, I used to, you know, shop for the groceries all the time and make sure the house is always stocked and make dinner every night and get the kids ready for school in the morning. And I still do that stuff. But a lot of times, you know, I let it slide. Sometimes I won't make dinner or whatever. And when I do do it, I just feel like I'm forcing myself to do it. The passion is gone.
Counselor: And how long have you been. You say housewife, right? How long have you been housewife?
Client: For a long time. I have two boys. They're eight and ten. And I've been staying home since my first one was born, so ten years. And, you know, it's been really rewarding for me. I'm not really interested in going back to work or anything like that because I know people always say you're feeling unfulfilled, like you should go back to work, but it's not, you know, I felt happy with it for so long. I don't think that it's being home. I think it's something inside of me.
Counselor: Something's changed. So for a long time, you were satisfied being a housewife. You enjoyed that life or found satisfaction in that life. And somewhere along the line, something changed in you and now you're not happy with it. So what it represents in terms of activities like caring for your children and shopping, now, that's what changed.
Client: Yeah, exactly. Well, I guess, you know, my youngest is eight, so he's only been in school for a couple of years. So I guess, like, it's not super recent, but recently I finally have no children in the home, so it's more. It's more time to myself, and I kind of filled that gap a little bit with other things. Like, I did Cub scouts with the boys for a while, and like I said, I had some friends around the neighborhood, so that kind of, like, filled that time. But now that stuff, it's just not really happening anymore. So now I kind of feel like it's not boredom. You know, it's not like I don't have enough to do. It's like I don't want to do anything, but then at the same time, I feel frustrated because there's nothing to do.
Counselor: All right, so you're frustrated with your situation, maybe with yourself a little bit?
Client: Yeah, I think a lot more with myself because I know that I would feel better if I had, you know, maybe found more friends or found something to do with my time, but I don't want to at the same time. So I'm frustrated with myself because I kind of know what would help, but then I don't really have the, like, the volition to do it.
Counselor: You're not motivated?
Client: Yeah, I'm not motivated.
Counselor: Have you received any feedback from other people about this meeting? Has anyone else noticed that you're down?
Client: Yeah, I mean, obviously my husband has noticed because he has to get the boys ready in the morning. He's really supportive. I know he can tell that I'm not feeling the same, but, you know, he works, and then he has to come home and pick up my slack. So he is getting frustrated, which I understand. And, you know, my mom has said to me that, you know, she thinks I'm not doing as much, and so it kind of hurts. It feels like everybody's trying to tell me I'm lazy and that I'm not doing enough. And it's always that, like, feeling, you know, like nobody really understands how much work goes into being a mother. But then, at the same time, now that I'm doing less and less, I feel like they're all right, you know? I am lazy. I'm not doing anything.
Counselor: They use the word lazy?
Client: No, not that I can remember. You know, I think my mom said, like, you're not doing as much as you used to. And I kind of took offense to that, even though it's kind of true. It's like. I don't know. It hurt.
Counselor: Okay. That was painful for you what about what your husband said? What's he been saying?
Client: You know, I think at first we didn't really acknowledge it. It was like, you know, I took a break here. He picked up the slack, and it was fine. But now that it's been more and more, he's kind of getting frustrated. And, you know, he's been asking me about how I feel and why I'm not doing as much. But at the same time, like, even though he knows that, not motivated, it's still frustrating because it's my responsibility. So I think he's. You know, he's been saying, like, I need you to do more around the house, pretty much is what he said. I need you to do more.
Counselor: What was your response to that? When he said, I need you to.
Client: Do more, I started crying because I know he's right. And that's what I tell myself every day. I need to do more, but I don't have the motivation to do it. And so I'm so frustrated with myself, and, you know, I know that he needs that from me, and I don't know why I'm not motivated to do it.
Counselor: Okay, so you're frustrated for feeling down.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you're frustrated for lacking motivation, and just as little as a few years ago, you didn't feel it this way at all.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. I actually think, you know, I've been feeling this way more, like, in the past, like, six months or something like that. Like, I. It was hard for me when my youngest son went to school, but more in, like, the natural way that it is hard, but this is something else. This is more consuming. It's, you know, like, the difficulty of him going away to school almost was motivating. Like, it was hard, but at the same time, it was freeing because I had other opportunities to do stuff. This is just, like, stunting.
Counselor: Okay, so let me shift gears a little bit. Can you tell me about your. Well, a recent day. It's kind of typical of what you're telling me now. Meaning not motivated. Down.
Client: Sure. On Wednesday, I was having a really hard time getting out of bed, so my husband just got the kids ready in the morning, and I felt really bad about that. So I just stayed in bed for a couple more hours, probably until, like, 1030, and I got up, you know, and made myself something to eat. And then I thought, you know, I should probably go to the store because we're almost out of milk and, you know, and I think the boys need shampoo. But I just. I just sat down and I just sat there, and I think I sat for. I don't even know how long the boys came home from school. It was like, you know, 330, and I hadn't even gotten up. And so then I said, okay, the boys are home. I should probably get started on dinner soon because my husband will be home soon. And I. I found something in the fridge to make, and I made dinner. And, you know, after that, everybody, you know, just sat down. We just watched tv, and I just sat there until it was time to go to bed.
Counselor: You said this was recently, right? What would the ideal day have looked like? Take that same day and do what you wish you could have done.
Client: I wish that I would wake up and, you know, I would want to wake up when it was time for the kids to get ready to go to school. You know, I could make sure that everything that they had, everything they needed, I could pack their lunches and get the boys dressed and, you know, check if they needed any permission slip sign, that kind of thing, send them out the door, and then I would see if we needed anything from the store. I probably do a little bit of cleaning around the house. I used to, like, have a list of chores that I would do different things on different days and different days of the month and stuff. So bedding would get washed one day of the week and that kind of thing. Probably, like, follow that list. Nowadays, I just, you know, if it gets done, it gets done. And usually my husband helps me with some of the stuff. And, you know, I would do the bathrooms one day a week. That probably gets done, like, once a month now, but I would do that. So do the cleaning. If we. If I needed to go to the store, I would do that. I'd get ready for the boys to come home. I'd probably make them a snack and figure out what was going to be for dinner. I would go ahead and do that, and then probably, you know, sometimes we would watch tv after my husband got home after dinner, or I would figure out something for us to do. We could play a board game, or I'll watch a movie as a family or something like that. But that would be after the kids did their homework and everything like that. And then after we spent some time together, I'd put them to bed.
Counselor: All right, so there's a fairly wide discrepancy between where you are in terms of behavior and where you want to be. So let me ask you a very specific question about one of the first things in the day. You had mentioned that when it was time to get up you didn't. So you were awake and aware of it, but you went back to sleep, I presume. And of course, your husband got up and he took care of things. How did you feel allowing that to happen? Because clearly that's not what you wanted to happen. How did you feel about that? Oversleeping?
Client: It's just like, you know, the alarm goes off and I know it's time to get up, and my husband's getting out of bed, and I just look at the clock and I think, what's the point? And, you know, it's just this instant feeling of. I can't even describe it, like pointlessness of getting up. And so I go back to sleep, but I feel worse for doing it, you know, like it's a catch 22. Like, I don't want to wake up. I just don't want to. But then when I go back to sleep, I feel bad. I feel guilty.
Counselor: Okay, so by not getting up in the time you wanted, you feel guilty. But you also mentioned something that you thought, which was, if I'm not mistaken, you said, what's the point? Can you expand on that?
Client: It just. It's just like, you know, when I'm sleeping, I don't realize how sad I am, and I don't realize how hard it is to function when I'm sleeping. I'm not aware of that. And as soon as I wake up, I am. And so I just have this feeling of, like, what's the point of getting up and experiencing these feelings when I could go back to sleep and not have to?
Counselor: What's the point of getting up when sleeping will keep the pain at bay?
Client: Yes. Yeah.
Counselor:
output: But then when you do get up, you feel sad and guilty about having overslept.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Victoria. How you doing today?
Client: Doing okay.
Counselor: Been doing okay. It's been a while now. You've been practicing with the waiting after you wash your hands? Mm hmm. How's that been going for you?
Client: Well, I think it's been going pretty well. I've been able to, you know, wait pretty good. I'm gonna start it out slow like you suggested, with three minutes. Then I would wash my hands for five minutes. I would wash my hands, and I got up to about 15 minutes.
Counselor: That's great.
Client: And there were some times that I was really proud of myself that I actually forgot.
Counselor: You forgot to wash your hands entirely?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So when was the next time you washed them?
Client: When I would go to, like, eat. Dinner,
Counselor: which is when you normally wash your hands. So really, you touched something that had germs, and you had some anxiety as you had to get to that waiting period. But then the anxiety subsided to a point where I forgot about it just wasn't a priority. You just completely forgot and went on with your day?
Client: Yeah. I was really proud of myself, but I got really concerned because I got sick. I got sick recently, and I'm afraid it's from one of those times that I didn't wash my hands.
Counselor: Well, tell me about the sickness.
Client: Well, my throat started to get hurt real bad, and I was just really congested. And all I could think about was, it's because I didn't wash my hands when I went to the store or when I went to my car when I touched a jacket. That's, you know, been everywhere.
Counselor: How many times do you normally get it? Sounds like a cold.
Client: I mean, it was kind of a light cold.
Counselor: Light cold.
Client: I mean, we wouldn't wait in a.
Counselor: Few days, a couple days. So how long or how many times a year would you get something like that normally?
Client: I mean, I get sick. I mean, quite often because of my job. I'm around a lot of people, and hand sanitizer can only work so much. I do get sick.
Counselor: So it's been six weeks since you started waiting? Right. I think it was around session three where we talked about putting a gap between when you touch something, when you wash your hands, like a time gap, and you got a cold once. Would that be out of the ordinary to get a cold one time in six weeks this time of year?
Client: I suppose not. I mean, the rational part of me knows that I get sick, but just because I'm trying something new with the, you know, and then the waiting and then the not washing, I'm just afraid that there was, you know, you're afraid.
Counselor: They were linked at one cause the other that waiting to wash your hands got you sick. And that could have happened. I don't know. But let's talk about the cold. You said it was a couple days.
Client: It wasn't severe. I mean, I took some, you know, over the counter medicine, slept it off.
Counselor: So wasn't a catastrophe.
Client: No, I've definitely been sicker in my life. And I mean, it did seem like one of those ones that I get every now and then.
Counselor: So when we spoke, I remember before you had said that the kind of worst case scenario, the reason that you're thinking so much about the germs on your hands is that it could make you sick. But you did get sick and you were able to tolerated.
Client: Yeah, I was. Which I found kind of odd because I was. I was panicked at the beginning when I started to feel those first, you know, the itchy throat, the headaches.
Counselor: Sure, it's miserable, right? Nobody wants to get sick.
Client: And I got concerned, you know, that it was because of that. Then it just kind of subsided. I guess I felt a little better, you know, as the days went on, I felt better about it happening, about.
Counselor: The whole getting sick and you started to recover. So kind of the worst case scenario occurred and you survived. And again, we don't know if the, the amount of hand washing you were doing before the ERP exposure and response prevention, we don't know if that would have prevented the cold or not. Yeah, because you do get sick several times, several times a year, in a year. So there's a lot we don't know. But we do know that you survived it and it wasn't as bad looking back at it.
Client: I mean, in my head, not washing my hands and the sick that I would get is a lot worse. It's like hospital worthy. And this was, you know, like I said over the counter, you know, relax a little bit.
Counselor: So not pleasant, but survivable.
Client: It definitely wasn't pleasant, but it wasn't as bad as it could have gone in my mind.
Counselor: So presume for a moment that it was a consequence of not immediately rushing over and washing your hands. What would you rather have? The occasional cold like that or the excessive hand washing and anxiety?
Client: I mean, I definitely don't like the excessive hand washing. I don't. I mean, it ruins my skin and I. It's expensive and it makes me feel bad about myself. And I mean, I guess the trade off is if I get a little sick and that would be okay.
Counselor: Again, that's presuming that it did cause you to get sick, which it may not have.
Client: I suppose that's true.
Counselor: So I wanted to point out, too, that I remember when we, we first started the exposure response prevention exercise, we did it right here in session by touching the arms of the chair. And I can see now your arms are.
Client: Oh, I didn't even notice I was doing that. Oh, I don't, you know, even noticing it, I don't feel like I need to go, you know, wash my elbows or anything.
Counselor:
output: You don't feel that compulsion?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, mister Urban. It's nice to see you again. From our previous session, I know you spoke about the relationship you and your wife were going through. In the bad terms, she got left off. So I want to ask you, what would make you cheat on your wife?
Client: You know, I've been asked that question every day for the past two, three weeks. And the only thing I can respond with is what would make a wife cheat on her husband? I mean, it's petty. I know it's petty. But I loved her. And finding out that more than once she was with somebody else, that took something from me that I couldn't get back. And for months I was dealing with. What could I have done? What was it? What did I do? Because it has to have been me. She's too nice a person for that, right? She's too smart a person for that, right? And then weeks of me finally understanding that it wasn't me. A decision that you make is a decision that you make. So when Susie, my administrative assistant, came into the picture, I had a decision that I had to make. I have to take it off and spend time with Susie. Or keep it on and spend many a night alone. So why? You figure it out.
Counselor: So do you think that you did it for revenge? Were you trying to get back at your wife?
Client: I guess. I mean, what else could it be? Yeah, maybe I am that petty. But it's just. It's not love anymore.
Counselor: So why are you still in a marriage, mister Urban? If it's not love, if it's not for love, why do you feel that you must stay in America?
Client: Because that's the type of household I was brought up in.
Counselor: Explain that to me.
Client: My dad always told me that you take care of your business and your girl is your business. You never leave her. You take care of her no matter what. That's what you do. So when I got older, I asked him, what do you mean you never leave her? He said, divorce is not an option. That's pretty much how it is in my household.
Counselor: So are you saying because of how you were raised up is why you're still in the marriage?
Client: It's the only thing that makes sense.
Counselor: Are you happy?
Client: Do I seem happy?
Counselor: Have you spoken to your wife about this?
Client: No. So everything that I feel, everything that I am is stuck on the inside. This is actually the first time I've actually talked about any of her.
Counselor: Okay, mister Ermen, so let's try this exercise. I'm gonna pull out chairs, so pretend that that this is your wife here. Why are we here and express your feelings.
Client: Why do I have to do this?
Counselor: Because you never spoke about it. Right? So express your feelings. Let it out, and see how you would tell her what you're feeling inside. Do you feel uncomfortable?
Client: I felt uncomfortable since the moment I found out that you just didn't love me anymore. I felt uncomfortable every single night I've been in the guest room because I just couldn't take being with you. I felt uncomfortable since the very moment I felt like it was okay because of what you did to me. To take off my wedding band, to forget my vows, to forget you, to try and be something that I'm not. Every night that I was with Susie, I imagined that I was with you, but not who you are now. I imagine that I was with the woman that I first met, woman that I first loved. But you're not the same person anymore. I haven't been the same person over a year. Every day that I wake up and I see your face, I have to imagine that you are that same person because that's the. The only thing that keeps me around. That and the fact that I just don't think I can make. And it's not because I love you so much anymore, because it's not you that I love. It's not because of anything religious. It's because I don't want to deal with my family.
Counselor:
output: I know that was hard to do. Mister Urban, are you doing all right? Are you feeling okay?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Samantha. How you doing today?
Client: Good, how are you?
Counselor: I'm doing all right. How have things been since last week?
Client: Things? You know, I've been really sort of preoccupied and anxious a lot this weekend. My daughter got sick, so I had to take three days off of work to take care of her. And I'm starting to worry. She's been sick a lot since I've gone back to work, and she's in daycare, and I've had to take a lot of time off work, and I'm getting close to going over my allotted amount of days. And so I'm finding myself being very anxious about that and then feeling guilty because when I'm trying to take care of her, I'm always worrying about work. So.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like a couple things may be going on. Child. Child's been sick, so you're taking off days. So you're a little worried about your relationship with your employer. At the same time, you want to make sure you're taking good care of your child, so you're having trouble reconciling those two.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right. What was the last time it happened? Can you describe what happened the last.
Client: Time I had to take off work? It was just this week. She woke up one morning with a really high fever, so I had to call out that day, and then she still had a fever the next day, and then I had to take a third day because she has to be fever free before she can go back to daycare. So the first day was, I was okay with that. But then, like, the second. And then when I started realizing that I was going to have to take a third day, then I really start to get kind of panicky and worried about it.
Counselor: All right, so let me see. Let's go through each day. So the first day when you discovered that she was sick, right. What were you thinking then when you had to call out of work?
Client: Well, because she's been sort of sick a lot lately, I was a little bit worried, and I was sort of, you know, I have this number, ten, because I only have ten days for the whole year. So I have this number in my head, and I just thought, well, there's one more day I gotta take away from that ten that I have. And. But I was able to sort of think about. I was a little worried about any work that I would miss, you know, keeping up with my caseload and stuff at work, so. But I was able to kind of figure out that I would be okay for a day. And I can kind of make up for that when I get back.
Counselor: Okay, so your thinking was, this isn't ideal, but I can live with it.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Just one day, right? How about on day two when you realize that you're going to have to take a second day?
Client: Then I got a little bit more worried. And then I did start to also, you know, add the worry of I was going to start to get behind at work. Not only was I missing more time, but I was also going to be behind on my work. So then I started thinking, when I go back, it's going to be a mad scramble to kind of catch up and keep up with everything and, you know, so then it became worrying about my workload and worrying about taking more time.
Counselor: Okay, so a little more stressful version of what happened on day one. And then how about when you discovered that you had to take a third day off?
Client: I was. Then it was just more amplified, you know, amplified worry. And it was a lot harder for me to let it go. I just kept thinking. I kept going back to it. And then I started feeling guilty because I was so preoccupied, worried about that. And I was trying to answer emails and do some stuff and send out some emails to people that I work with to try to help me out with things at work since I wasn't there. And then I felt guilty because I wasn't really caring for my child as best as I felt I should have been. You know, I started feeling kind of like a bad mom.
Counselor: So, so guilty and a bad mom. And that was mostly on the third day? That was the worst of it, yes. Now, did this go up against the weekend? It was the third day, Friday. So then you kind of knew that by Monday things would be able to return to work. So tell me what happened when you returned to work on Monday.
Client: Well, I checked in with the main office and, you know, I just said, I'm really, you know, I'm starting to worry. I'm getting. I know I had to take a lot of time, but you. I've done the best I can to try to make other arrangements, but just starting back in, starting in daycare, she's just been sick a lot and I can't control it. I'm doing the best I can. I asked them if there was anything I needed to do as far as providing doctor's notes and stuff, and they said, no, they don't need a doctor's note since it was my daughter that was sick. They said there's nothing, nothing that I really can do and just try to not have it happen much more if I can just do what I can to not miss more.
Counselor: So they said that to you?
Client: Yeah, but. Yeah.
Counselor: How did they frame that?
Client: They kind of just said, you know, do what you can to not have it happen, but if it, you know, if it has to happen, you know, what can I do about it? It's kind of. They were saying.
Counselor: So they were understanding.
Client: I didn't feel like they were that understanding, but I also didn't feel like they were gonna take any punitive action against me. Right. Right then and there or anything.
Counselor: Did you anticipate a worse reaction than you experienced?
Client: Yeah, I did. And I also anticipated that they would maybe have more of a procedure for how to handle it, and they didn't have a procedure, which also made me feel a little worried. I can't imagine I'm the first mom that has had to deal with this. And they kind of talked like it's never happened before, so I kind of felt anxious because I thought, am I really the first mom that's had to take a lot of time off because their child's sick? They didn't give me the impression that they had sort of a protocol or like they had dealt with this before.
Counselor: Right. So sort of like it took them by surprise.
Client: Yeah. Or they just didn't have a plan for what to do about it.
Counselor:
output: They weren't investing a lot of energy in thinking about that?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Emma. How you doing today?
Client: I'm doing good.
Counselor: Doing good?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What's been going on?
Client: I've been a little anxious about a shopping habit that I have.
Counselor: Yeah, tell me about that.
Client: Well, I have to buy everything in pairs or in twos. And if I only have one thing, I won't buy it. I'll put it back or I'll look around the store for another thing so that I have two things to buy.
Counselor: Oh. So when you go into a store, if you just have one thing you want to buy one item you went there for, you will buy a second item or even more or just a second.
Client: Sometimes it can be more as long as it's reached the minimum of two.
Counselor: So you have to leave having purchased a minimum of two.
Client: Right.
Counselor:
output: Or if you can't find something else, you won't buy it at all.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Tony, you've been given this diagnosis of schizophrenia by one of your doctors. I just wondered what it's like for you and what the main problems are.
Client: The main problem is these. Well, they tell me that it's a problem to do with musketsophrenia. These voices, they come and they. I heard these people talking about me and talking about how rubbish I am and what a failure I am, and I really just wish they'd leave me alone.
Counselor: Yes, that's extremely negative content to what's being said. So it's a clear voice outside of your head, is it?
Client: Yeah, yeah, it's two voices. And, you know, sometimes they're talking to me and sometimes they're talking about me, but it's always really negative. There's no helpful things there at all.
Counselor: It sounds like these voices are associated with a feeling of sadness. Am I getting that right or is that another feeling?
Client: Oh, well, when I let them, they get me really down. They get me really, really down. But, you know, I'm fighting these. Fighting them still, you know.
Counselor: What are you doing to fight?
Client: Well, there's where I get into a real problem, because I shout back at them. And, you know, my neighbors, they. Well, you know, they don't understand and they say they don't hear these voices. Sometimes I wonder if my neighbors are in on it as well, but, you know, they say that they can't hear them, but I don't understand how they can't hear them because they're so loud.
Counselor:
output: So loud.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hazel, how you doing today?
Client: I'm okay.
Counselor: What's been going on?
Client: Well, last time I started to tell you a little bit about one of my friends, my best friend, actually, she had this issue. So what happened was she went to a bathroom at our local library, and she found a video camera when she was going to the bathroom.
Counselor: In the bathroom?
Client: Yeah. She actually. Yeah. And she turned it into the police, and I guess because, like, she carried it, or she had found it, her handprints were on it, and they weren't be able. They weren't able to detect who actually did it. They weren't able to catch the person.
Counselor: Oh, they didn't catch the person?
Client: No. So since then, I've been on really just high alert. Like, I'm worried that that could happen to me, to my kids, and I'm just really worried because they didn't catch the guy, that him or someone like him could be out there.
Counselor: So he's still out in the community.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So how is it affecting your. Your daily life? Can you tell me kind of what your. What you've been feeling?
Client: Um, a lot of anxiety just not knowing, maybe, you know, what if someone were to videotape me like that? I've been very aware, shall I say, of cameras.
Counselor: Okay. So anxious and aware.
Client: Right. Like, I know you have one in your office, and people on their cell phone cameras. Just all the possibilities that I could be recorded. I've just been very aware of them, which makes me not want to go anywhere. So I've been having arguments with my husband a lot because he wants to go out to restaurants, and I don't want to go because there could be cameras in the bathrooms and how I dress. Also, as you can see, I'm kind of dressed more conservatively because I remember hearing once about cameras that people use on shoes that could be used in a creepy way. And so I can't. You know, it's now almost summertime. I can't dress in skirts or be comfortable because I'm dressing like that.
Counselor: So you covered a lot of ground there. So you have the. You have the feeling of being, like, worried, nervous. Right. That's going to happen to you, but you've also had to kind of change your routine, or you feel you have to change your routine to feel safer.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Has that helped. Has changing the way you dressed or changing where you go and when you go, has that helped reduce the anxiety?
Client: Not really, no. I would say it's really starting. That's why I wanted to come in. It's really starting to affect my life.
Counselor: You mentioned specifically your husband. Like, what's been going on there?
Client: He just wants to go places with our kids, like, go out to eat. And I don't really want to go anywhere because, you know, cameras are everywhere nowadays, and I just kind of worry, like, public bathrooms, could they be there? Could someone be, you know, sometimes baby monitors are, you know, hooked up on so people can hack into that laptop, cameras. So even in my own house, I've just been really nervous, so I feel like I'm not really getting relief from that anxiety.
Counselor: Have you taken any precautions because of this persistent worry? I mean, I already mentioned, like, with the camera specifically.
Client: I mean, I've, you know, when I go into bathrooms, I've been looking for cameras to make sure they weren't there before. You know, me or my children have used the bathroom. I have tried. I read online that you can turn how to turn off the cameras on your phone and that you can close your laptop, and that way the camera will face down. And the same thing on a smart tv so it doesn't recognize your face. I've tried to turn things off. They don't need to be on as far as people being able to access my own information.
Counselor: And that seems reasonable. So you take reasonable precautions to try to avoid being video recorded against your will.
Client: Exactly.
Counselor: Okay. But still, you have this feeling of worry, anxiety, and your schedules being interfered with.
Client: Right.
Counselor:
output: So you'd like to cope more effectively with your feelings, reduce this anxiety. So when you enter into a public bathroom. Now, we talked about automatic thoughts before.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Okay, Marsha, so how can I help you today?
Client: Well, I'm working full time. I'm a part time student. I've just gotten engaged, and I live at home. There's just so much stress in my life. I have everything happening all at once. Just to top it all off, I failed an exam, a really big exam, and I just feel like I can't do anything anymore. I can't do anything right. I've just got so much stress, and I feel like such a disappointment, such a failure. And I've embarrassed my family by failing. I just don't know what to do anymore. I guess I've come here today to tell you, like, I want to leave uni, and I guess that's why I've come here to you today.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like a whole lot of stuff's on top of you at the moment.
Client: Yeah, just so much. Just all parting on. Yeah.
Counselor: So you're working full time, plus part time study. Part time study. And then you've got your wedding preparation.
Client: Yeah, just got engaged, and weddings just a month away now, so, yeah, so I've just got so much happening. Work is really, really demanding and. Yeah, just fail this exam. It's just. Yeah, don't know what to do all too much.
Counselor: So imagine you've been sweating on this for a while, and it's all been swirling around in your head.
Client: Just been building up and building up and so much pressure with everything. And I'm living at home, so my parents, you know, a lot of pressure, need to do everything right. And. Yeah, by failing this, I feel like I've just embarrassed and disappointed them, and I just don't feel like I'm good enough, you know, to go on studying.
Counselor: Okay. And have they said much to you about failing your exam?
Client: They haven't said much. I was really scared to tell them, actually, because I knew they'd just be so disappointed and just embarrassed by the fact that I did fail. Yeah. I've never failed anything before. And so, yeah, really hard.
Counselor: Yeah. So it's new and you don't like it at all?
Client: Not at all, no. And I think leaving uni will just be the way out, just so I don't have to go through it again.
Counselor: Right. Okay. Well, I'm glad you've come to counselling, because it's good for us to get an outsider's opinion when we've got so much on our plate and we're confused as to what to do and our emotions can get in the way. And you've just said earlier that a whole lot of stuff's on your plate at the moment. Okay. So I'm glad you've come here. Here at the clinic, we use the ABC model, which is a cognitive behavioural therapy model. So, Marsha, some counsellors have put together a list of beliefs that we often use and we don't realise that we're using those beliefs and they tend to be faulty ones. Here's the list. Here, have a look through that to see if there are any beliefs that you might be operating on at the moment.
Client: I think number two.
Counselor: Okay, read that one out for me.
Client: That it's necessary to have a high degree of order uncertainty in order to be happy and perform well.
Counselor: Yeah, yeah, you mentioned that earlier.
Client: Number four, that it's necessary to be competent and successful in all those things which are attempted.
Counselor: Yeah, that's an expectation from your family.
Client: Yeah, possibly. Number eight, that life should be entirely pleasant and enjoyable and that any frustration, discomfort or pain would be unbearable.
Counselor: Which one of those stands out the most for you at the moment?
Client: Um, probably number four.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: How would you put that in your own words?
Client: That I need to be successful all the time in everything that I do. Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. And is that different from what's happening in your life at the moment?
Client: Well, failing that exam, I mean, I wasn't successful with that. So. Yeah, I mean, it just throws out, I guess, even number two because throws out all the order in my life. I need to have everything, you know? So I need to know what I'm doing, where I'm going. Yeah.
Counselor:
output: So, okay, so if number four is an expectation that your family have and that you have of yourself, how do you measure up next to number four?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Alisa, how you doing today?
Client: Good. How are you?
Counselor: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. How has the anxiety been going since last session?
Client: It seems to be in check. Nothing really major has been going on with it. So I think I'm getting to a point where it's under control.
Counselor: It subsided a bit. That's good. That's good. How's things been going at work lately?
Client: So work's a little bit of a different story. We have our daily meetings, and. I. Actually had to pull, like, one of my coworkers aside because I feel like they undermine me all the time, and they, like, they don't give me the respect, basically, that I deserve. So I took her outside after the meeting and leaned into her about it. And afterwards, I mean, the next day, because we have these meetings every day, she, like, she came back and came at me again, but it was worse even after talking to her.
Counselor: So talking to her, that didn't improve your situation?
Client: No.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Well, Meredith, we know each other, but the way we usually start a CBT session is to set an agenda. So we might have several ideas about what we want on the agenda. But the first thing is usually for us to make a problem list together about whatever it is that you might want to work on.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: And then we'll do the problem list, and then we'll explain, explore the thoughts and the behaviors that might be related to the problem. And hopefully, by the end of our time together, we'll have a clearer idea about what's causing the problem and some ideas about how to maybe change things.
Client: Sounds good.
Counselor: All right.
Client: So one thing that I've been noticing lately is that I have a tendency to kind of hang back in groups, and I tend to observe instead of participate.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: And a lot of times I get really nervous when I feel like I'm expected to speak up. And I want to speak up, but I kind of feel like I freeze.
Counselor: Okay. And so in particular, then, in groups, the setting is big groups, little groups. Does it matter?
Client: It doesn't matter a whole lot, but generally, I guess medium size. Like, you know, in classes that I have usually, like maybe twelve people or so. So relatively small, medium. I don't know what size that is.
Counselor: Okay. And so. But in your head, you probably would say, I would like to speak up, but for some reason, you feel inside some anxiety or nervousness about that.
Client: Definitely.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: And then sometimes when I try to force myself to speak up, when I actually don't feel ready, I get like. I feel like my throat's closing and I get a red face.
Counselor: Okay. All right. So that's sort of one possible issue for us to talk about. Could you maybe give me a specific example of a particular group situation, as recent as you can, where you had this feeling of hanging back and maybe. Maybe some fear of evaluation?
Client: So in my statistics class each week, we have a. It's called an inclusion activity. And generally, I guess it's supposed to help people feel like the group's more cohesive and included, but I usually experience it as the opposite. So there's usually a task at the beginning of each class of like, take off your shoe and talk. Talk about the most interesting place your shoe has been. Stuff like this in stats that, um, usually I get really nervous and I feel like I can't think of anything to say. And I feel like I usually end up saying something really awkward or lame, and I just don't feel good about it. Like, I feel.
Counselor: Yeah. Can you give me that specific example of the recent time when maybe. And then. And what you said, too, including sort of the beginning, what happened and then how it ended.
Client: Yeah. So when we did this activity, it's, like, a really weird example. When we did this activity, you know, probably six or seven people had gone in front of me, and I was, like, not listening to anything that anyone else was saying, just totally self absorbed in terms of, like, oh, God, what am I going to say? And not being able to think of anything. And then when it was my turn, I was wearing a pair of shoes that, like, are kind of, like, they have lace on them. And so I took it off and I said, I like these shoes because I get cool tan lines from them. So I didn't even really answer the question that was like, where have these shoes been? Or, like, the coolest place these shoes have been? Or something like that. And then after I went, I didn't really listen to anything else anyone said because I was still, like, stuck on, why didn't I answer the question and just kind of feeling awkward.
Counselor: Okay, so what I'm doing here is I've got several columns that I'm building, and the first one is, you're in the stats class, and you're going through an inclusion activity. And the second one is the thoughts that you're having. What thoughts are going through your mind? And the thoughts are, oh, God, what am I going to say? Those are the early thoughts. And then maybe the later thoughts are, why didn't I even answer the question?
Client: Yeah. And, like, why can't I ever be articulate?
Counselor: Okay. Why can't I ever be articulate? Okay. And then our third column are the emotions that you might be feeling. And so as you're in that situation and people are taking their turn, the teacher says, you're doing the inclusion activity. People are taking their turns. And what are you feeling? How would you describe your emotional state?
Client: Nervous. Yeah. Like, fearful. And, like, it's almost like I'm anticipating. Anticipating embarrassment.
Counselor: Mm hmm.
Client: So I don't know that's a feeling or not, but usually I feel embarrassed.
Counselor: I put that in the thought okay. Column just because it seems like the anticipation of it is probably a thought, but embarrassment when you're in the middle of it is probably a fear. Does that make sense? And then. So I got nervous, fearful, embarrassed as the emotions, and on a scale of zero, not at all. 100 being the most of that feeling you could ever have, how would you rate? Let's get rid of nervous because it's sort of covered by fearful. How would you rate fearful. And how would you rate embarrassed?
Client: Maybe fearful? Like a four. Okay, four or five. I don't know.
Counselor: Four out of five.
Client: Out of 140.
Counselor: Okay. I was gonna say. Oh, feeling pretty calm. So a 40 or a 50?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. And embarrassed.
Client: I'd say that's higher.
Counselor: A little higher.
Client: Yeah. Like a 70.
Counselor: So maybe a 70. And that would be at the moment that you're talking or right afterwards or right before fluctuating?
Client: Yeah, I'd say, like both during and after.
Counselor:
output: Okay. Okay. So during and after. Alright. And so, you know, the cognitive approach to thinking about what's going on is that it's not the situation that causes the emotional reaction, but it's what you're thinking that causes the emotional reaction. And so it seems to me like one of the things that's going on. Oh, God, what am I gonna say? And why didn't I answer? Why can't I never be articulate?

Client: I don't know if there's a certain level, but I feel just like I deserve it. Mm hmm.
Counselor: You know, and what did she do that kind of convinced you that she wasn't meeting that level of respect?
Client: Well, she was, like, shooting down my ideas and just kind of made me feel like a fool, basically. So I just. I didn't understand.
Counselor: All right, so she had criticisms of your ideas, right? A few of them, it sounds like. So that would upset anybody. But were those criticisms unusual, given the tone of these meetings? Like, is this a type of meeting where people criticize each other or attempt to in a constructive way?
Client: I mean, I guess.
Counselor: Have you criticized other coworkers?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So do you think that her criticism was within normal limits, like, within the. What you've kind of seen there regularly?
Client: I mean, now that you pointed out? I mean, I guess I can view it in that way that it wasn't.
Counselor: It wasn't too far out of line the first time. Right. But then after you talked to her, you said that it got worse.
Client: Yeah. So it just felt like she was purposely trying to nitpick, if you will.
Counselor: Trying to get at you a little bit.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So maybe the second time around, correct me if I'm wrong, maybe she was actively showing you disrespect just because of what you had done, because you came after her. Or was that with the normal limits, too? I don't know.
Client: I mean, I. I guess I may have gone at her a little harshly, but I felt at the time that.
Counselor: It was reasonable at the time when you were.
Client: When I was talking to her outside of the meeting.
Counselor: All right, so you felt that she was a bit harsh. You talk to her about it, but then she's become more harsh. So where do you stand with her now, like, with the meetings?
Client: Well, I've just been trying not to talk to her, and obviously in a work situation, doesn't really help.
Counselor: That's not convenient. Yeah, it might not help. All right, so let's work this through. Using the ABC model, like we used for the anxiety that you had before that was troublesome to you before. What would the activating event be here in this situation?
Client: So I guess the confrontation I had with her.
Counselor: Well, you could look at that as an activating event. Another way to look at it is her criticism of you could have been the activating event, and your conversation with her could have been the consequence. But these things are cyclical, so it's sometimes hard to know where to cut in and put the a and the b and the c. But let's just work it through with the activating event being what she said. Let's just try that, okay, and see how that works out. Would that be reasonable? That could have been kind of what started it was this criticism.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: All right. So then what would the belief. So all activating events, right, are filtered through our belief system. So what would your beliefs be in that scenario?
Client: So she criticized me, and I felt disrespected.
Counselor:
output: That's a feeling.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Alex, we're going to continue today with the trauma memory task like last time. So this is, of course, you talking about your memory of the attack from beginning to end in as much detail as you can. Just to remind you, we've said that we are doing this to help put this memory sort of back into the past, I guess, where it belongs. We hope that by doing this, it's going to help lessen those nightmares and flashbacks and other upsetting memories of the attack that are bothering you quite a bit at the moment. So how do you feel about that? About going through the memory again together today?
Client: Can't say I'm excited about it, but I'll give it another shot.
Counselor: Yeah. Look, I think we do know that this is difficult right now. But what I also expect is that it's going to get easier and easier for you to talk about this memory the more often you do. And I'll be right here with you to support you with that. So, same as last time, I'm going to ask you to talk about the memory as if it were happening now. So in the present tense. And I'm going to ask you to start at the bit where you are waiting for the tramdhead and end it at the part where your mum is there or your mum arrives. And I'll be checking in with you about where you are on the thermometer again. So before you begin, where are you in terms of your distress on that zero to ten thermometer?
Client: I'm about a five.
Counselor: About a five?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay, well, let's go through that memory again, starting whenever you're ready.
Client: So I'm sitting playing with my phone at the tram stop. I see them out of the corner of my eye. Two guys wearing jeans, hoodies and sneakers. I don't think much of it. Then they come up behind me, grab my arms and put them behind my back. My phone smashes to the ground. I can feel my heart pounding. I'm thinking, oh, God, what are they gonna do to me?
Counselor: Okay, you're doing well. Where are you on that thermometer?
Client: About a seven.
Counselor: Okay, stick with it.
Client: Then. I feel something cold metal on my neck. I realize it's a knife. I think, oh, shit. Then one of them whispers into my ear, give us your watch or I'll stab you. I can smell booze on his breath.
Counselor: You're doing well. Where are you now?
Client: Eight.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: I'm too paralyzed to speak. I just try and nod. They let go of my arms, but the knife is still there. One of them takes the watch off my arm. Then they start going through my pockets. I guess they're looking for cards or money. He finally puts the knife away. Then they pull me onto my feet and one of them knees me so hard in the stomach that I fall back down. Then they start kicking me in the stomach and just run off.
Counselor: Ok, you're doing well. Where are you on that thermometer now?
Client: About a seven.
Counselor: Keep going if you can.
Client: I'm lying on the ground in pretty bad shape. I can't breathe properly. I'm thinking, I don't have my phone. How is anyone gonna find me? Are they gonna come back for me?
Counselor:
output: Okay, doing well. Where are you on that thermometer?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Jean. How are you?
Client: I'm good.
Counselor: So this is the second time that we've seen each other. Right. You came in for the initial assessment about a week ago now, I think, and I got to know you and your history and kind of the symptoms that you've been dealing with, and it seems like you've been struggling with depression. Is that. Does that sound right?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Yeah. So between, you know, last time you were here and now, did anything come up, anything positive, anything challenging?
Client: Yes. When I try to pull weeds, it just takes me forever in my garden, and then I have to come in and sit down, and then I just don't understand why I can't do it like I used to, and it's frustrating.
Counselor: Okay. So is that. That's related to the medical issues that.
Client: Yes. I have arthritis in my knees and my back.
Counselor: How long has that been going on for?
Client: Oh, really bad for the last, like three years. So.
Counselor: And that's been kind of a difficult adjustment. You were really active before, right?
Client: Yes. I could do all my gardening one day and not have to stop. And now I have to stop. And it's.
Counselor: So what do you think about all that?
Client: I hate it. It's like, why? Why can't I do it? You know?
Counselor: Yeah. Yeah. Well, it is. It's a big difference when you are, you know, not experiencing physical pain and you can do all these things that you enjoy and then something happens, you know, as we're getting older, it always does. So, yeah, it can definitely present a lot of challenges. Anything else happened in the last week?
Client: Well, I've been wanting. I need to go walking more often, and I just can't. It just bothers me, my knees and. And I get frustrated because I can't do that and.
Counselor: Okay. And then, you know, when you get frustrated and you can't do something, what do you do after that?
Client: I, um, just sit there and usually get up and eat something, and that's not good for me when I'm trying to lose weight. So then.
Counselor: Oh, I see. So it's kind of like a cycle. You want to do good things for your health and exercise, but it's been challenging because of your medical issues. And then it kind of leads you to overeating, which is kind of counterintuitive to your goals.
Client: Right. It's like, why. Why am I eating this?
Counselor: Well, you may have noticed that I ask a lot of questions about what you think about things and how you feel about things. You know, in the first session you came in, and then today I just kind of wanted to point out how cognitive behavioral therapy works. That's the kind of therapy that I actually do and will be using together to kind of hopefully help you get through this time to where you feel like there's some improvement in your mood and how you're feeling. So let me just start by drawing a little diagram using an example that we just talked about together. So say a situation comes up like, you go to pull the weeds in the garden. I'm going to write pull the weeds in the garden. And then you said you were able to do it, but for a short period of time before pain kind of got in the way. Right. And then when that pain got in the way, what was the thought that you had?
Client: It's like, why do I have this pain? Why? Before, I never did. I should be able to do this, but I can't.
Counselor: Okay. So I got, you know, why do I have this pain? And I should be able to do this. So then after you had that thought, what did you feel? What emotions came up for you?
Client: Frustrated, sad, and I get anxious.
Counselor: Okay. And then after you felt those things, the frustrated, sad, and anxious, that's when.
Client: I would eat the ice cream.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Our sweets, candy, whatever.
Counselor: Okay. So I kind of put this in a model to show you how cognitive behavioral therapy works. So all these different situations happen, and different people see them in different ways. So when you had, you know, this situation come up where you went to go pull the weeds in the garden and you couldn't do it as long as you wanted to, you had this kind of, like, more negative, self critical thought going on. I mean, you were able to go pull some of the weeds even if you weren't able to do as much as you wanted to. But because, you know, you kind of had these negative thoughts, it led you, it affected your emotions, and then in turn, it affected the behaviors that you did afterwards. And what we find in cognitive behavioral therapy is that we have the most control over our thoughts. You know, what we think of an event. Like I mentioned, we could think like, oh, well, you know, at least I was able to do this much. You know, I can give myself a rest. My body's telling me to take a rest, and then I can go back to it again. So that's kind of what our target is going to be. And it all starts with identifying these automatic thoughts that you're having, these quick reactions that are happening in your brain. And it seems very simple, but it is, you know, challenging to do. So that's what we're going to start off working on. Did that all make sense?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Okay, good. So I have this worksheet here that you can take with you and we'll get going on our first step in working together. So right here there's a lot of columns, but I really only want you to worry about the first three columns. And this is going to get you tracking what automatic thoughts are coming up for you. So we've got date and time, the situation or event that happened, and then automatic thoughts. So maybe we can go through one more because you did mention walking as well, right. That was also a challenge for you. So when was that you were going to go for a walk?
Client: Well, I was going to go yesterday and then I just. I just couldn't because my knees started. I just get out the door and can't even get down the steps sometimes.
Counselor: Oh, that must be difficult.
Client: Yes.
Counselor:
output: Right. And then I'm gonna put for the situation. Couldn't go for a walk. Alright. And then do you remember what thoughts you had?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Tony, you've been given this diagnosis of schizophrenia by one of your doctors. I just wondered what it's like for you and what the main problems are.
Client: The main problem is these. Well, they tell me that it's a problem to do with musketsophrenia. These voices, they come and they. I heard these people talking about me and talking about how rubbish I am and what a failure I am, and I really just wish they'd leave me alone.
Counselor: Yes, that's extremely negative content to what's being said. So it's a clear voice outside of your head, is it?
Client: Yeah, yeah, it's two voices. And, you know, sometimes they're talking to me and sometimes they're talking about me, but it's always really negative. There's no helpful things there at all.
Counselor: It sounds like these voices are associated with a feeling of sadness. Am I getting that right or is that another feeling?
Client: Oh, well, when I let them, they get me really down. They get me really, really down. But, you know, I'm fighting these. Fighting them still, you know.
Counselor: What are you doing to fight?
Client: Well, there's where I get into a real problem, because I shout back at them. And, you know, my neighbors, they. Well, you know, they don't understand and they say they don't hear these voices. Sometimes I wonder if my neighbors are in on it as well, but, you know, they say that they can't hear them, but I don't understand how they can't hear them because they're so loud.
Counselor: So loud.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor:
output: What do you make of these voices, then? Do you think it's part of an illness, or do you think the neighbors are doing it? Or what do you think?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Carly. How you doing today?
Client: Doing okay.
Counselor: You doing okay?
Client: I guess, yeah.
Counselor: Not sure.
Client: I don't know, just the same.
Counselor: Yeah, still a little down.
Client: Yeah, I've been sleeping a lot. Going to work is a struggle. I don't really ever want to go. Just I haven't been eating much, so I think I've lost like ten pounds since past, like four months or so.
Counselor: Past four months?
Client: Um, just the guy. I don't know, I just haven't really been doing anything.
Counselor: You still been working?
Client: Well, yeah, yeah.
Counselor: But not much else?
Client: No, I usually just go to work and go home.
Counselor: Tell me what happens after you arrive at home, like after work?
Client: Um, well, my fiance tries to talk to me and really I just kind of want to go to sleep for just. I don't know. I tried, I tried reading the other day. Cause I used to like that and it's just, I think I got like into two pages and put the book down and decided to go to bed.
Counselor: What were you thinking when you put the book down?
Client: Just that I wasn't really happy doing it. I didn't really get any enjoyment out of it.
Counselor: I. And before you were depressed, which is, I guess about eight months now, you did enjoy reading?
Client: Mm hmm. Oh, yeah, all the time.
Counselor: So what would you have thought if you had to put a book down back then?
Client: Oh, I used to fall asleep reading. I would be up till like two in the morning just reading a book.
Counselor: Something you look forward to?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But not now?
Client: No, I just didn't really get any. I just wanted to try it and then I put it back down and was like.
Counselor: Were there other things that you used to enjoy doing that you don't feel motivated or comfortable to do now?
Client: Yeah, I used to be a runner and then I tried going for a run the other morning with my dog and I. I think we walked a block and that was pretty much it. I just couldn't wait for it to be over.
Counselor: Alright, so it wasn't a pleasant experience. Was there any part of it you connected with when you were running, like when you first started?
Client: Not really. I mean, it was a change to be outdoors and I realized I hadn't really seen the sun in a while, so. But other than that, I just, I had the intention of going out to run. I had my running shoes on and my dog was really excited. And then by the time I got out there, I was like, yeah, we're gonna walk. And then I thought about walking like our normal route. And by the time I got to the corner, I was like, yeah, we're gonna turn around and walk back.
Counselor: So what was the feeling like when you returned to your home after planning to run and then kind of walking and coming back?
Client: Kind of a mix of, like, relief just because it was over, and then, I guess more sadness because I didn't do anything. I didn't do what I had intended to do.
Counselor: Sadness, maybe disappointment.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So I've seen you a few times now, and based on those conversations, and, of course, what you said today, it seems like you have, for a variety of reasons, given up on the activities that you used to enjoy, you're not motivated toward them anymore.
Client: Yeah, I guess you could say that.
Counselor:
output: And that's a common symptom of depression. I think we've talked about this a little bit before. So it's tough when you're depressed to find joy, satisfaction, happiness in activities that you once enjoyed. So we've been working with the cognitive piece. Right, like we did last time, we talked about the automatic thoughts that come up and kind of how that leads to some of the feelings of sadness and what we can do with the self talk. I'd like to talk about a different technique today that approaches the problem from a different angle. We'll continue to work the cognitive angle, but I want to add a new angle. And the technique is called behavioral activation. The theory behind it is that if you engage, if you schedule and engage in activities that you once enjoyed, even if you kind of have to fight your way through it a little bit, like with the running, that will connect to your mood. Right. Remember, we believe in cognitive therapy, that affect and behavior and cognition are all connected. So what you're thinking affects your behavior and your mood and what you do. Your behavior affects your thinking and your mood. Does that kind of make sense based on what we talked about?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.

So I was hoping we could start there with what happened that made you afraid of this dog.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Liz. How you doing today?
Client: I'm alright. How are you?
Counselor: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. What's been going on in the last week?
Client: It's still the same. Nothing at home is going right. It's. I'm still yelling, we're still fighting.
Counselor: Like you and your boyfriend.
Client: Yeah. He just can't get it together. He can't. He doesn't do anything right. He doesn't. And I just end up screaming every day and it takes it all out of me.
Counselor: All right, so he can't do anything right. And you're arguing, being angry every day?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So what are you taking away from this? Like, what do you think's going on?
Client: I feel like he does nothing wrong and I end up screaming at him when I come home from work, and that's a lot out of me every day, and I don't want to feel angry every single day.
Counselor: That's what's happening.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What types of things do you think are triggering your anger response?
Client: It's anything. It's. I come home, he's just sitting on the couch. I've had a long day at work. He gets homework before me, and the dishes aren't done. Nothing's, like, thawed or even started for dinner. And is that just supposed to be my, like, it's not. He could just do one thing and I just. I just lose it. I lose it and I can't. I can't control it. I just started screaming at him that he does nothing, that he could just do one thing for me. He could just have the sink clean, empty one thing, and it. Every single day. And then the next day it's something else. The trash is now, like, you name it.
Counselor: So every. Every day when you come home from work, there's something he's done or failed to do that triggers yelling?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What's his response to this? Like, what's he doing when you yell at him?
Client: He gets mad back. He just starts screaming back at me. Like, I expect too much and I get too upset and why am I always yelling at him? Why can't I give him the benefit of the doubt?
Counselor: I'm.
Client: But I don't understand it. Like, you could do one thing and then. And I just. I can't help it. I scream at him.
Counselor: Are there other things he does at other times that you feel are helpful? Or is it. Or is it always, like, when you come home, is it always something that hasn't been done right or hasn't been done?
Client: I mean, on anniversaries, whole make dinner. So that's nice.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: He makes good money. So that's. He keeps that together.
Counselor: Okay, that's about it.
Client: Yeah. The rest is just. I just get angry at him.
Counselor: So if you were to pick adjectives to describe him, what adjectives might you. Might you select?
Client: Stubborn, condescending, and intelligent.
Counselor: Intelligent, stubborn, condescending, and intelligent. Do you see him as this way kind of all the time, or is this change?
Client: I don't think it's all the time. Like, there. Like sometime, like a month ago when a friend at work died. Old age, whatever. But I had a long day. He knew it beforehand. I didn't have to say anything. When I came home, everything was good. There was no trash, no dishes. So it's not all the. All the time, but just lately, it's just. I had no words.
Counselor:
output: So lately it's all the time. Yeah, but there's been prior occasions when this hasn't been a problem. Yeah, but there's not many of those. So after you have, you yell and argue, what's it feel like to you then? Like, what's your mood?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Carly. How you doing today?
Client: I'm good. How about you?
Counselor: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. How did you do this week?
Client: Better. Well, last time we talked about that postpone gratification. Yeah, that, and I think you wanted ten minutes for me to put it off.
Counselor: Ten minutes, yeah.
Client: So I did better. I think I ended up only doing, like, a joint a half instead of two. I was able to put it off for, I think, the ten minutes a couple times. And then I. There was, I think, one or two days where I went out for a walk because I was tired of staring at the clock, waiting for the ten minutes to pass. So I got up, went for a walk, and then I passed one of my friends, so I ended up walking with her. And I actually didn't get back to my house for, like, an hour, so I kind of put it off for, like, an hour because then I came home and took a couple hits.

Client: It was rough, yeah.

Client: Yeah.

Client: Yeah, I found I actually, like, talked to a couple people on the phone. Before I knew it, like, a half hour had gone by.

output: So another activity presented itself. And you forgot about the marijuana?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Client: Hi.
Counselor: What brings you in today?
Client: Well, I recently moved, and I just feel really alone and just unhappy.
Counselor: So I'm hearing you feel lonely and unhappy. What's causing those emotions?
Client: Well, I completely alone. I have no friends at all. I just feel at a loss. I've tried making friends, but it's just been super difficult. No one seems. I just don't really have a lot in common with people. And I don't know, I just kind of go home each day, don't even have a job right now, and it's been really just depressing, to say the least.
Counselor: Now, where were you moving from?
Client: I was moving from Los Angeles.

Client: I'm by myself.
