instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, mister Urban. It's nice to see you again. From our previous session, I know you spoke about the relationship you and your wife were going through. In the bad terms, she got left off. So I want to ask you, what would make you cheat on your wife?
Client: You know, I've been asked that question every day for the past two, three weeks. And the only thing I can respond with is what would make a wife cheat on her husband? I mean, it's petty. I know it's petty. But I loved her. And finding out that more than once she was with somebody else, that took something from me that I couldn't get back. And for months I was dealing with. What could I have done? What was it? What did I do? Because it has to have been me. She's too nice a person for that, right? She's too smart a person for that, right? And then weeks of me finally understanding that it wasn't me. A decision that you make is a decision that you make. So when Susie, my administrative assistant, came into the picture, I had a decision that I had to make. I have to take it off and spend time with Susie. Or keep it on and spend many a night alone. So why? You figure it out.
Counselor: So do you think that you did it for revenge? Were you trying to get back at your wife?
Client: I guess. I mean, what else could it be? Yeah, maybe I am that petty. But it's just. It's not love anymore.
Counselor: So why are you still in a marriage, mister Urban? If it's not love, if it's not for love, why do you feel that you must stay in America?
Client: Because that's the type of household I was brought up in.
Counselor: Explain that to me.
Client: My dad always told me that you take care of your business and your girl is your business. You never leave her. You take care of her no matter what. That's what you do. So when I got older, I asked him, what do you mean you never leave her? He said, divorce is not an option. That's pretty much how it is in my household.
Counselor: So are you saying because of how you were raised up is why you're still in the marriage?
Client: It's the only thing that makes sense.
Counselor: Are you happy?
Client: Do I seem happy?
Counselor: Have you spoken to your wife about this?
Client: No. So everything that I feel, everything that I am is stuck on the inside. This is actually the first time I've actually talked about any of her.
Counselor: Okay, mister Ermen, so let's try this exercise. I'm gonna pull out chairs, so pretend that that this is your wife here. Why are we here and express your feelings.
Client: Why do I have to do this?
Counselor: Because you never spoke about it. Right? So express your feelings. Let it out, and see how you would tell her what you're feeling inside. Do you feel uncomfortable?
Client: I felt uncomfortable since the moment I found out that you just didn't love me anymore. I felt uncomfortable every single night I've been in the guest room because I just couldn't take being with you. I felt uncomfortable since the very moment I felt like it was okay because of what you did to me. To take off my wedding band, to forget my vows, to forget you, to try and be something that I'm not. Every night that I was with Susie, I imagined that I was with you, but not who you are now. I imagine that I was with the woman that I first met, woman that I first loved. But you're not the same person anymore. I haven't been the same person over a year. Every day that I wake up and I see your face, I have to imagine that you are that same person because that's the. The only thing that keeps me around. That and the fact that I just don't think I can make. And it's not because I love you so much anymore, because it's not you that I love. It's not because of anything religious. It's because I don't want to deal with my family.
Counselor: I know that was hard to do. Mister Urban, are you doing all right? Are you feeling okay?
Client: I'm fine.
Counselor: Okay. So I want you to realize, like, can you not see that your belief is causing this pain inside your depression and your unhappiness?
Client: It makes sense, if that's what you're saying. The question is, how am I supposed to deal with, like, right now? I know I've got the option of staying with her and dealing with this every day for as long as I stay with her and deal with this or just leaving, and then I have to deal with everything else around me. How am I supposed to get past that? That's my question. And I don't know. I don't even know if that's really the right way to go.
Counselor: What is everything else?
Client: My family, the judgments. What? I'm gonna have to deal with my brother, who, by the way, is married, and he's not dealing with infidelity, but he's dealing with the same depression I am. The love isn't there anymore. We don't get divorced. Not in my household.
Counselor: So would you rather satisfy what, your family standard? Rather to be happy? Is that what you're saying?
Client: Sounds like it.
Counselor: Have you spoken to your family about this?
Client: No.
Counselor: And what do you think they would say if they were to find out.
Client: That I was thinking this way? My dad would probably disown you.
Counselor: To go that far and disown you.
Client: Especially when I seen that he dealt with the same thing. My family doesn't do well with marriages because I haven't met a single person in my lineage that has a happy marriage.
Counselor: Do you see your family often, Mister Urban?
Client: Not really.
Counselor: Do you want to be happy, mister Urban?
Client: Who doesn't?
Counselor:
output: So do you feel like if you left your wife and were to move to a different place, would you be happy?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:

Client: I'm doing okay.
Counselor: Doing okay?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What's been going on?
Client: Well, nothing too bad. I kind of got in a little bit of a. Like, a fender bender accident.
Counselor: A car accident?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What happened?
Client: Well, we were at a stop sign, and I was, like, actually a red light, and there was one car here, another car here, and then I was here, and the car was behind, coming up behind me, and then they hit me, and then I hit the car in front of me.
Counselor: Oh, yeah? You okay?
Client: I kind of, you know, you know.
Counselor: Just the usual rock back and forth.
Client: Yeah, yeah.
Counselor: But other than that, you're okay? No, I got a couple, you know.
Client: Little bruises from, like, hitting the steering wheel. I'm like, yeah, but I'm. I'm okay. My body's okay.
Counselor: So, physically, you feel okay?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Were you, like, checked out by your physician or anything?
Client: Yeah, everything's okay here. I didn't break anything or pull anything.
Counselor: How about emotionally?
Client: It's been kind of hard to, like, be, like, get in my car again afterwards. Like, I've been still been going to work and everything, but, like, I realized last night, like, my boyfriend was like, oh, do you want to go on a trip this weekend? And I was kind of, like, maybe not. Like, I'm kind of, like, hesitant to get back in the car.
Counselor: So when he said that about the trip, what was the thought that came in your mind?
Client: I'm gonna get hurt.
Counselor: So it was really all about the car?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: It wasn't anything else about the trip?
Client: No, it was driving. It was being in the car. Driving the car, yeah.
Counselor: I thought was, you're gonna get hurt.
Client: Yeah, I'm gonna get hit. I'm gonna get hurt.
Counselor: Yeah, yeah. Any. Any other areas? So it disrupted that trip. So you normally would have went, oh, definitely.
Client: I would have been really excited about it. But this now I'm just like, no, I don't know. Or, like. Or even, like, coming here. I was like, well, maybe I can reschedule. Like, I was just like, oh, I don't want to drive. I don't want to. I don't want to be behind the wheel. I don't want to drive. And, like, when I did drive, I was. I was fine coming like I would. You know, I drove the way I normally do, but I was a little bit more aware. But I. You know, I wasn't driving extra slow. I wasn't driving extra fast or anything, but, like, I was checking a lot more. I. You know, but very nervous.
Counselor: Very much more nervous than usual.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: How did you feel about driving cars prior to this accident?
Client: It was fine. I mean, whenever, like, my friends and I would go anywhere, I would always volunteer drive. Like, I. Like, I enjoy driving. I, like, listen to the radio. You know, I like my family and I always went on trips. And, like, as soon as I turned 16, like, I always had a turn. I, you know, I enjoyed it, like, going on drives, just, you know, looking around, but now I don't. Too scared. It, like, doesn't even. Doesn't even come in my mind anymore. It's, like, a thing I would want to do. If I can avoid it, I will.
Counselor: So you're taking every opportunity to avoid driving so far, getting, like, here today and getting to work, sensual functions you've been able to do.
Client: Yeah, it takes me. It takes me a while to actually, like, okay. Like, I have to, and then I just kind of do.
Counselor: So what do you tell yourself to motivate yourself to get into the car? Like, to come here today, for instance?
Client: Well, it takes me. I have to kind of think about it for a long time. But, I mean, I'm very nervous. I mean, I don't. I can't even really think of what I tell myself. It just kind of happens.
Counselor: And when you get in the car, like, when you kind of work past that nervousness and get in the car, how do you feel then?
Client: Still pretty scared. Yeah, I'm pretty scared throughout the whole thing. I'm always worried that, like, if I can go away, that I know that doesn't have any stoplights, I'll try to go that way, even if it takes me an extra half hour.
Counselor: Oh, that long?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor:
output: Well, how about now? Like, you've driven here, I presume you're gonna drive your own car to wherever you're going next.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.

output: It's that bad? Yeah, really intense. So would you. Would you think that you were a more accurate evaluator of what's true or not now or when you're in that state of anxiety?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Tony, you've been given this diagnosis of schizophrenia by one of your doctors. I just wondered what it's like for you and what the main problems are.
Client: The main problem is these. Well, they tell me that it's a problem to do with musketsophrenia. These voices, they come and they. I heard these people talking about me and talking about how rubbish I am and what a failure I am, and I really just wish they'd leave me alone.
Counselor: Yes, that's extremely negative content to what's being said. So it's a clear voice outside of your head, is it?
Client: Yeah, yeah, it's two voices. And, you know, sometimes they're talking to me and sometimes they're talking about me, but it's always really negative. There's no helpful things there at all.
Counselor: It sounds like these voices are associated with a feeling of sadness. Am I getting that right or is that another feeling?
Client: Oh, well, when I let them, they get me really down. They get me really, really down. But, you know, I'm fighting these. Fighting them still, you know.
Counselor: What are you doing to fight?
Client: Well, there's where I get into a real problem, because I shout back at them. And, you know, my neighbors, they. Well, you know, they don't understand and they say they don't hear these voices. Sometimes I wonder if my neighbors are in on it as well, but, you know, they say that they can't hear them, but I don't understand how they can't hear them because they're so loud.
Counselor: So loud.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What do you make of these voices, then? Do you think it's part of an illness, or do you think the neighbors are doing it? Or what do you think?
Client: Well, you know, I think there was somebody once that I really didn't get on with at school, and I think it's him. And I think he's kind of got these people to be kind of harassing me. I think they're trying to drive me mad, I think, is what they're trying to do.
Counselor: That's a very distressing experience. I can understand that. So do you think other people can hear them if they're very loud?
Client: Well, you know what? They say they can't, but that makes me wonder if they know what they're. If maybe they're on it. But everybody says that they can't. And, you know, I don't know. I've tried my CPN said, you know, why don't I put a recorder on, you know, when the voices are there and, you know, it didn't pick them up, but I don't know. Maybe it was faulty or something. It just nobody else can hear them, I guess, is the answer to your question. Or everybody says they can't.
Counselor: Even with the tape recorder, you still don't think. Well, you think other people maybe can see them, hear them?
Client: Well, sometimes I think people can hear them, and sometimes I think, you know, well, maybe my CPN's right. Maybe it's my imagination.
Counselor: So is it just you that hears voices, or do other people in society hear voices, Tony?
Client: Well, there's somebody else at the day center, and he hears voices that other people can't hear. And we've talked together, and I can't hear the voices that he's hearing.
Counselor: That's interesting, isn't it?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And I wonder if there's certain types of stress which can make anybody hear a voice. Have you ever heard of that kind of a thing? No, because quite often, soldiers coming back from the war will be hearing the sounds of battle, gunfire and helicopters, etcetera. So they're not actually there, but they hear them as if they're real, and it's linked to the stress of being in a war. Do you ever find that your own voices are worse if you're not getting asleep, if you're sleeping really badly?
Client: Definitely, definitely. What I find is that sometimes when I get really worried about what they're doing to me, and I think, well, maybe I'll stay up just in case they're going to pull some tricks or something in the night. And times when I do that, actually, I do hear them more the next day.
Counselor: So maybe lack of sleep has something to do with voice hearing. And this is very commonly seen in society that the longer that people stay awake, the more liable they are to hallucinate. What about drugs? Are the certain drugs that cause voices? What do you think?
Client: I don't know. I guess I've heard people talking about being a bit paranoid when they take cannabis, but I don't know whether that would be.
Counselor: I mean, there's other types of drugs that make you see things like taking LSD or anything really nasty like that.
Client: Yeah, I've heard of that.
Counselor: Can really make you hallucinate things that aren't actually there. So there's lots of possible causes. It seems like the human brain can very easily hallucinate under certain conditions, and there are certain things that can keep that hallucination going. So it seems like about 8% of society will have a period in their life of hearing the kind of voices that you're hearing, Tony. But the vast majority of them will get better again. 8%. 8%. So it's a very common human experience. But at the far end of that 8%, there's a group of people with a diagnosis of schizophrenia because their voices are so distressing. They're hearing them day in, day out, and they're really affecting their life. So that is where that kind of label comes from. Basically, everybody at some point has had some kind of hallucination, whether it be hearing things, seeing things, feeling a touch.
Client: How do you know that?
Counselor:
output: Well, it is said, tony, that following grief, you know, when someone close to you dies, as you grieve over the loss, there's always a phase of hallucination. And during that phase, you will either see that person or you'll hear them speaking to you, or you'll smell a perfume or an aftershave or feel their touch. And after you've finished grieving, it doesn't happen anymore.

Well, you've said a couple things here for disputing. One is that, hey, I'm taking too much on. And then I also. I wanted to pick up also and kind of just on the cycle and the cycle of relationships and that we do tend to kind of go through a little bit of a roller coaster with some folks and, you know, with some folks, it's a little less hilly, but sometimes we feel closer to people at certain times in our life than others. There's a developmental aspect, I think. What else am I missing here? If we're disputing, you say, hey, I'm taking too much on. Oh, he's also. He's.
Client: Yeah, he could.
Counselor: He's responsible, too. Okay. So you kind of come up with that kind of stuff, and I'm curious how that works for you. The disputing part.
Client: I guess just thinking about it from that point of view, it makes it easier to handle. I don't know, it makes me feel, like, a little bit better, I guess, about myself.
Counselor: Okay. Okay. So kind of keeping those thoughts in mind that I'm taking too much on here. He can make a phone call. He can help us straighten this out. Kind of the general cycle of relationships. Keeping that stuff in mind helps you feel less sad.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: On that scale again, where would you put yourself if you can keep that in your mind?
Client: Maybe like a three. So, like a little bit better. Like, I think I'd still be sad that we don't have as close a relationship right now.
Counselor: Yeah. Yeah. So you can feel that. But then there's. I guess what I'm sensing is there's less personal responsibility for it. So it's. So it sounds like that helps. Yeah. And helps a little bit. Yeah. And I guess the trick is what you do to kind of maintain those thoughts because it's real easy to get back into the habit of, oh, God, it used to be.
Client: Yeah, yeah, yeah. I think it is really easy to fall back into those old thought processes. So I guess just, I don't know, reminding myself that, like, maybe comparing to other relationships and. Okay, remember how you're talking about, like, the cycle.
Counselor:
output: Cycle. Okay. So kind of expanding and thinking about other relationships you have and even thinking.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.

Counselor: So has this been something that you've struggled with for a long time, or are you just noticing this recently?
Client: A long time, but I kind of avoided social situations where I had to.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: So it was just, like, a reminder that I'm just a super awkward person.
Counselor: Okay, so what are some of the feelings that are associated with that feeling super awkward?
Client: I think, like, embarrassment and just, like, weird. Like, I feel like people are just, like, not wanting to be my friend.
Counselor: So you almost feel, like, what sounds like possibly not being accepted?
Client: Mm hmm.
Counselor: Okay. Has anyone ever made you feel that way before?
Client: Um, I can't remember a time. No. I think I just, like, feel I'm so embarrassed and made such a fool in myself that I don't, like, pursue that friendship as much. Okay.
Counselor: You feel like you're going to make a fool of yourself, or you felt.
Client: Like, when I first meet them, if I was, like, a super awkward silence, I feel so embarrassed, I don't want to talk to them again.
Counselor: So awkward silences, that's one that really causes some anxiety for you. Anything else that makes you really anxious before talking to them? Some of those fears you have?
Client: I think I'm very self conscious about maybe how I look. I think I'm very concerned about, like, how I present myself to people, that I'm always trying to figure out what to say, if that makes sense.
Counselor: And how do you think you look from your perspective?
Client: I don't know. I think I'm just. I think it's more of how I want, like, how I think other people do. Like, I feel like I'm fine, but I feel like other people may not think I'm attractive, and so I feel like they don't want to be friends, but, like, an unattractive person.
Counselor: So you think that other people think that you're unattractive, but you feel fine about yourself.
Client: Mm hmm.
Counselor: So can you kind of tell me what you think is fine? What do you mean by that?
Client: Like, my appearance. I mean, I think I'm like, a cute person. But I also know, like, everyone has a type and, like, a certain group of friends they want. Maybe I don't fit into that. Mm, tight.
Counselor: Okay, so when you said that, that you think you're a cute person, you gave a smile. So it seems like you really believe in that, which is great. So can you give me a number from zero to ten? What you think about yourself? That you're fine, that you're kind of cute. Zero being not at all pretty ugly, or I don't really believe in that. And ten being I'm certain I'm confident in this. And I think I'm pretty cute.
Client: Maybe like, a seven and a half.
Counselor: Seven.
Client: Five.
Counselor: That's really good.
Client: Eight. Seven and a half. Okay.
Counselor: Either one. That's a pretty good number. A pretty strong number. So it seems like you have pretty good self esteem on your end as far as how you value yourself, but it's the fear of how other people value and think about you. Okay. And so is the only concern of people thinking that you're not good looking, unattractive, or is there other concerns too?
Client: I think just the attraction thing is just always in the back of my mind and kind of affects how people talk to you. So I feel like I have to cater around their judgment. Yeah. So it's just hard for me to initiate conversation without knowing, like, what they think about me. Okay.
Counselor: So you're just what? Sounds like you're just kind of thinking what they might be thinking of you, but you don't know. But with you not knowing, that causes.
Client: That anxiety, and it would just be awkward for me to ask them directly, like, what do you think about me? Okay.

Counselor: Yeah. Look, I think we do know that this is difficult right now. But what I also expect is that it's going to get easier and easier for you to talk about this memory the more often you do. And I'll be right here with you to support you with that. So, same as last time, I'm going to ask you to talk about the memory as if it were happening now. So in the present tense. And I'm going to ask you to start at the bit where you are waiting for the tramdhead and end it at the part where your mum is there or your mum arrives. And I'll be checking in with you about where you are on the thermometer again. So before you begin, where are you in terms of your distress on that zero to ten thermometer?
Client: I'm about a five.
Counselor: About a five?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay, well, let's go through that memory again, starting whenever you're ready.
Client: So I'm sitting playing with my phone at the tram stop. I see them out of the corner of my eye. Two guys wearing jeans, hoodies and sneakers. I don't think much of it. Then they come up behind me, grab my arms and put them behind my back. My phone smashes to the ground. I can feel my heart pounding. I'm thinking, oh, God, what are they gonna do to me?
Counselor: Okay, you're doing well. Where are you on that thermometer?
Client: About a seven.
Counselor: Okay, stick with it.
Client: Then. I feel something cold metal on my neck. I realize it's a knife. I think, oh, shit. Then one of them whispers into my ear, give us your watch or I'll stab you. I can smell booze on his breath.
Counselor: You're doing well. Where are you now?
Client: Eight.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: I'm too paralyzed to speak. I just try and nod. They let go of my arms, but the knife is still there. One of them takes the watch off my arm. Then they start going through my pockets. I guess they're looking for cards or money. He finally puts the knife away. Then they pull me onto my feet and one of them knees me so hard in the stomach that I fall back down. Then they start kicking me in the stomach and just run off.
Counselor: Ok, you're doing well. Where are you on that thermometer now?
Client: About a seven.
Counselor: Keep going if you can.
Client: I'm lying on the ground in pretty bad shape. I can't breathe properly. I'm thinking, I don't have my phone. How is anyone gonna find me? Are they gonna come back for me?
Counselor: Okay, doing well. Where are you on that thermometer?
Client: I'm about an eight.
Counselor: Okay, keep going.
Client: I feel like I'm there forever, but finally I hear a guy calling out. He's asking him if I'm okay. I couldn't get any words out, so I just make a weird sound. He comes over. He's an older guy, about 50. He says everything's gonna be okay. And I'm so relieved I start crying.
Counselor: Where are you on that scale now?
Client: About six?
Counselor:
output: Yeah, yeah, keep going.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.

Client: I still catch myself, like, double, almost like double touching. Like going to touch it and then reeling back. So I'm starting to notice it, but I still, I still have that anxiety. I still don't want to touch it.

Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What are some things that you've touched in the last, between the last session and this session that have distressed you?
Client: Well, I had to go to the store, which is always a nightmare for me because I don't even like touching my credit card because it's been in so many machines and there's so much dirt and junk that gets in there and then the counters and all the. I keep thinking about the food that's there, and I, you know, if I pick it up off the shelf, how many people have picked it up with their nasty hands or kids picked it up with nasty hands and then put it back, and it's like, I need to eat. But shopping's a nightmare for me.

Client: Yeah, everything does.
Counselor: Everything does. And that's what you're thinking about as you're walking through and shopping. We talked about last time, exposure and response prevention, and I explained kind of the general idea. But you remember that conversation. Yeah, I remember. I indicated that we might try some experiments right in session to see how, see if we can move kind of forward and treating your, kind of your fear and obsession with germs and really the anxiety it's causing for you, it's like getting in the way of your life.
Client: It is. It really is.

Client: I'm really not liking the covers on this chair because, I mean, I can't. I mean, at least what I'm sitting in now, my clothes are protecting me from the rest of the chair.
Counselor: Mm hmm.
Client: But, I mean, I have no sleeves on, so I don't like touching the armrests and the covers.

Client: To go wash my arms until I feel like it's gone. Until all the dirt is gone.
Counselor: And how long would that take you to be sure?
Client: I mean, something like this, probably. I'd probably be in there for a good 510 minutes. Just washing.

output: 510 minutes. How many times a day would you end up washing your hands?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Alisa, how you doing today?
Client: Good. How are you?
Counselor: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. How has the anxiety been going since last session?
Client: It seems to be in check. Nothing really major has been going on with it. So I think I'm getting to a point where it's under control.
Counselor: It subsided a bit. That's good. That's good. How's things been going at work lately?
Client: So work's a little bit of a different story. We have our daily meetings, and. I. Actually had to pull, like, one of my coworkers aside because I feel like they undermine me all the time, and they, like, they don't give me the respect, basically, that I deserve. So I took her outside after the meeting and leaned into her about it. And afterwards, I mean, the next day, because we have these meetings every day, she, like, she came back and came at me again, but it was worse even after talking to her.
Counselor: So talking to her, that didn't improve your situation?
Client: No.
Counselor: So you have these. Someone understands. You have these daily meetings, and you mentioned that she's not showing you respect and that you deserve respect, something to that effect. So tell me about that belief. Remember we talked about ABC before, activating events and beliefs and consequences in rabt. Tell me about that belief.
Client: Well, I just feel that I do a good job and I deserve to be respected by my coworkers. Yeah, it just.
Counselor: Are there levels of respect? Is there a certain level of respect that you demand or need?
Client: I don't know if there's a certain level, but I feel just like I deserve it. Mm hmm.
Counselor: You know, and what did she do that kind of convinced you that she wasn't meeting that level of respect?
Client: Well, she was, like, shooting down my ideas and just kind of made me feel like a fool, basically. So I just. I didn't understand.
Counselor: All right, so she had criticisms of your ideas, right? A few of them, it sounds like. So that would upset anybody. But were those criticisms unusual, given the tone of these meetings? Like, is this a type of meeting where people criticize each other or attempt to in a constructive way?
Client: I mean, I guess.
Counselor: Have you criticized other coworkers?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So do you think that her criticism was within normal limits, like, within the. What you've kind of seen there regularly?
Client: I mean, now that you pointed out? I mean, I guess I can view it in that way that it wasn't.
Counselor: It wasn't too far out of line the first time. Right. But then after you talked to her, you said that it got worse.
Client: Yeah. So it just felt like she was purposely trying to nitpick, if you will.
Counselor: Trying to get at you a little bit.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So maybe the second time around, correct me if I'm wrong, maybe she was actively showing you disrespect just because of what you had done, because you came after her. Or was that with the normal limits, too? I don't know.
Client: I mean, I. I guess I may have gone at her a little harshly, but I felt at the time that.
Counselor: It was reasonable at the time when you were.
Client: When I was talking to her outside of the meeting.
Counselor: All right, so you felt that she was a bit harsh. You talk to her about it, but then she's become more harsh. So where do you stand with her now, like, with the meetings?
Client: Well, I've just been trying not to talk to her, and obviously in a work situation, doesn't really help.
Counselor: That's not convenient. Yeah, it might not help. All right, so let's work this through. Using the ABC model, like we used for the anxiety that you had before that was troublesome to you before. What would the activating event be here in this situation?
Client: So I guess the confrontation I had with her.
Counselor: Well, you could look at that as an activating event. Another way to look at it is her criticism of you could have been the activating event, and your conversation with her could have been the consequence. But these things are cyclical, so it's sometimes hard to know where to cut in and put the a and the b and the c. But let's just work it through with the activating event being what she said. Let's just try that, okay, and see how that works out. Would that be reasonable? That could have been kind of what started it was this criticism.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor:
output: All right. So then what would the belief. So all activating events, right, are filtered through our belief system. So what would your beliefs be in that scenario?

Client: I'm good. How are you?

Client: I've just been feeling kind of in a rut. I mean, I've been looking for a job and haven't really gotten anywhere. And I just felt like such a loser because that was the time that I should have been at work if I had a job, and instead I was at the bar drinking. So I had one drink, and then it led to another. Cause then I just felt worse and I figured I had one, so.
Counselor: All right, so how much did you drink in total?
Client: I think I lost track after four or five.
Counselor: How long had it been since you had a drink before that?
Client: I did really well. It was, I think, like three weeks.
Counselor: Three weeks?
Client: Three weeks or so.
Counselor: Oh, so you did really well and then you had one drink and that just made you feel like you weren't successful?
Client: I felt like a loser.
Counselor: Felt like a loser. And you feel that kind of led to drinking some more? So you had a rough time with things?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. How about now?
Client: I mean, now I just kind of. I don't know, I'm afraid to go back. Like, I'm afraid to go out with, like, some friends. They invite me out to dinner, but I know there's alcohol and.

Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right, so there's a few things going on. We've talked in the past, right, about separating the behavior from the person. Right. So behavior is what we do, not who we are. But it sounds like when you had that first drink, you're kind of ashamed that you had a drink and you had it during the time when you would have been working.
Client: Yeah, that's pretty accurate.
Counselor: That's pretty accurate. So, taking yourself back to that moment, right. We had that first. That first drink, like, you finished that first drink. What was your thought at that moment?
Client: Just, like, shameful. Like, I did really, really well, and then here I was, and I had just finished a drink, and I knew I wanted another one.
Counselor: Okay, so shameful is kind of like the feeling, but the thought is I did really, really well. Right. So that's what you're thinking was, I did really, really well. And what was that the end of the thought? Or was that. Was there more before you had that next drink?
Client: I guess just I was doing well, and then I had a drink, and I just felt like an awful person. So figured what was the. The hurt and having more.
Counselor: So the sequence would have been you had the drink, you felt shameful. At the same time, you're thinking that you were doing really well, and then just really, as you said before, you just felt like a loser. And then you decided, might as well just have the second drink. So another thought might be that, like, I might as well, just might as well just have a second drink.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. So you can see how there's some thoughts and some feelings at work. Right. As you finished that first drink, was it fairly quick? Were those thoughts and feelings fairly occur fairly quickly after the drink?
Client: Yeah, I would say as I was finishing and then finished.
Counselor:
output: Right away, you regretted it. And in that regret, as you thought about it, thought, might as well just continue drinking now because you kind of blew it.

Client: I guess like 9500.

Client: Just like quite a lot of things. Like I wouldn't have anyone sit at lunch or people's birthdays and stuff. I wasn't invited and you know, like I was the last one picked for teams and stuff like that.

Counselor: Do you have, like, any type of severance or anything like that?
Client: No, no, no. So, yeah, I. It's just, you know, they let me go. I have really nothing to go on. I don't know what to do. I've been at that job so long, I really don't know how to do anything else.

Client: Yeah.

Client: I'm not sure. I'm still looking into that.

Counselor: Hi, Hazel. How you doing today?
Client: I'm okay.
Counselor: You okay?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I know when we met last time for your intake, you were concerned about some presentations that you had to give at school.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: You want to talk about that today?
Client: Yeah. So in school. I am in school for teaching, and we have to give presentations a lot, as you can imagine, on different things. And so it's something that's recurring. And what happened was I gave a really bad one one time. Yeah. I wasn't feeling very well, and I gave. I think I was just supposed tired from studying all night, and I gave a really bad presentation. And then, like, now, ever since, like, when I've tried to give subsequent presentations, I am just so nervous and I'm up there, like, sweating and, like, starting to forget what I'm gonna say. And I'm just, like, a fear of getting up there and having to get a presentation because I feel like I'm gonna bomb it.
Counselor: All right, so was there a time before, like, recently, when you had to give presentations?
Client: Yeah, I mean, like, before, earlier in my. Like, I'm towards the end of my degree, so, you know, throughout my program, I have. I have.
Counselor: And how did you do with those?
Client: Pretty well. I mean, I consider myself a pretty good student. So normally I do pretty well, it seemed, you know, come out of nowhere.
Counselor: So this presentation that you gave with the. Where you received a poor score, maybe just an isolated incident?
Client: Yeah. Like I was saying, I wasn't. I wasn't feeling very well, I don't think. And it really hasn't happened.
Counselor: But that experience has still led to a lot of anxiety with subsequent presentations.
Client: Oh, yeah. Like, I'm worried about my grades suffering as a result, and, you know, how well I'm going to do.
Counselor: All right, so would it be okay if we kind of step through the whole process of you giving a presentation? Sure. Right before I start with that, is this something that leads to anxiety, like, right now or other times or really just in that moment when you're presenting?
Client: Mostly it's most intense in that moment. And, like, maybe, like, leading up to it, like, in preparation that I know that this is gonna happen. Like, I always know when I'm gonna present. Like, it'll be like, the teacher will say, oh, well, you know, you're this Thursday, someone else is next Thursday. So the closer it gets to that event, the more anxious I am. Like, in anticipation.
Counselor: Okay, so you start feeling anxiety a few days before presentation.
Client: Yeah, I would say a few days, mostly.
Counselor: When does it start to get really distressing for you?
Client: Like, two days before or one day before? Then I'm like, oh, my gosh, like, am I ready? Like, what if I mess up? You know, what if I get a bad grade? All these, like, what ifs.
Counselor: Okay, so would you be okay if we step into this process and kind of break down the steps of the presentation? Yeah. All right, so let's say that you're taking. What's one of the classes you're taking now?
Client: Early childhood.
Counselor: Early childhood. So let's say you have a presentation in that class a few days from now. Just a normal presentation. So let's now move to two days out, where you would start to feel a little anxiety about it.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor:
output: What's going through your mind at that two day out point?

input:

Client: I'm alright. Thanks for actually seeing me today. Sure.
Counselor: How have you been? I know last time I spoke with you, you were having some difficulties at work.
Client: I'm still having difficulties at work and that's why I'm glad I have a session today because it hasn't stopped. The frustration and anger is just, it's there ten times more than normal.
Counselor: You're really frustrated. Way more than normal, way more angry.
Client: Yes, it's, there seems to be a lot that's going on and I continually don't get the help that I need, not only not from my coworker, but also my supervisor. So it just feels so that everything is my responsibility and I have to make it happen. And if I don't make it happen, it's not going to happen. And then it's just, it's all on me and I don't feel as though that it's fair. But I also don't want us to not succeed. So I don't know how to navigate those two field.
Counselor: So the weight of the work assignments is really on you. You're feeling that pressure. You want to do right by your employer and there's an emotional toll this is taken on you. Has it reached a point where you've talked to your, it's a coworker supervisor you mentioned?
Client: Yes. So I talked to my supervisor about my coworker actually assisting me with some of the projects that we have going on. And my supervisor keeps on saying, oh, they're helping out and they're doing what they're supposed to do, but they're not doing what they're supposed to do because I end up doing their work. Because, say, for example, last week we actually had to turn in this huge report that we were working on for over a month. Literally, my coworker came to me on Monday and said I didn't do my portion of the report. And I was just like, we had a month to work on a lot of time. And so I spent the next three days doing everything for their part of the report. Luckily, I had already finished my part of the report and then combined it and actually turned it into my supervisor. Counselor: If you both contributed equally.
Client: Correct? Correct.
Counselor: So in three days, you made up for a month's worth of work.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So I could see how that could be. It's very stressful.
Client: Very, very taxing. Very, very taxing.
Counselor: And this wasn't an isolated incident?
Client: Oh, no. This has been going on for probably three or four months now.
Counselor: So this is almost the expectation when you get to work.
Client: Correct? Correct. I think that you hit the nail on the head. It's expected of me and nobody actually sees it as an expectation anymore.
Counselor: It's just what you do. It's just what I do. So you can know that going into work the next day, you go in, whenever that is, that there's always this probability, this chance that you could have work just thrown on you that wasn't budgeted for, you weren't planning on.
Client: Correct. And sometimes that work actually comes out from my supervisor, but it's mostly coming from my coworker. Like, I know they're not going to do their portion, so I just automatically start doing it anyway because, you know.
Counselor: You kind of have to.
Client: I know it's going to fall on my lap either today, tomorrow, next week. So I would rather be preemptive and actually start it then so that I'm not rushing like I was, like last week to finish a month's worth of work and three days worth of time. So I'm not as stressed.
Counselor: So you've tried to address this in the framework, in the context of your work. You've talked to the supervisor, to the co worker?

And my supervisor keeps on saying, oh, I'll fix it, or, oh, it doesn't seem as though that they haven't done their piece of the work because I do all of it and it's turned in. So I have. Counselor: What kind of options, in terms of your job do you feel like you have now?
Client: I don't feel as though that I have any options. That's the thing. I think that either if I can, if I don't do the work and we fail, we're going to lose some of these big projects that we're working with, which then is going to impact our entire office. And if it impacts our entire office, like somebody might be let go. And because I am the newest person in our office, I feel as though that's going to be me. So I need to protect my job by doing not only my work, but my coworkers work and sometimes my supervisors work.
Counselor: So you're really figuratively fighting for survival?
Client: Correct.
Counselor: Do you think your coworker is aware that if there is a failure with getting projects done, that you would be the one that would be let go?
Client: I think, yes. I think that they understand that since they are the senior member on team, it would be most likely that the junior member myself would possibly be let go if a budget cut were to happen.
Counselor:
output: So you're really largely stuck.

Client: Yeah.

Client: Not really. I mean, it's pretty much the same pace. I'm very frustrated with the whole system. I'm working with inner city kids, african american kids, males in particular. And, you know, I sit and talk with these kids and I realize that there's not much I can do for them. You know, for the most part, we're talking about, you know, criminal arrest, drug abuse, you know, no education. And, you know, I don't know what I can really do for them anymore. And this kid has absolutely no life skills. None. He's self medicating or smoking marijuana. At the very least, it's marijuana. And, you know, anything other than this is not even, you know, I didn't fathom. So I'm sitting here, just kidding, I'm trying to draw him out of that whole mindset. But we're talking about years of social conditioning, years and years and years of it. And I just don't know if, you know, I have the skills and the tools to really break through that way of thinking.
Counselor: All right, so can you think of a particular case, particular youth that you're working with that, where you're finding the struggle. I just think of one particular individual where you're frustrated, you're making these statements that kind of. This is the way it is. They don't seem like they have much hope. You don't seem like they have much hope for them. Right. So you have one in mind.
Client: Yes, they do.
Counselor: Okay, so what's his self statement? What's he saying to you that you think is getting a reaction from you?
Client: That he's a drug dealer. He's going to continue to be a drug dealer. He's not going to stop. And that he's involved with gang activity, and that's his family. It's the only family he's ever known, and he's loyal to them. And that loyalty is deep. And he has absolutely no. Even the thought of going back to prison doesn't shape this kid.

Client: I don't know.

Counselor: You're not a mind reader. I mean, he probably didn't even know what was going to happen over the weekend. You think about all the other people who would have seen clues in some way. You know, Laura. Laura saw the poem. Laura saw the artwork. Chris and the art department, they were raving about the artwork. You know, no one was to know. And even myself, you know, I knew about. instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Tony, you've been given this diagnosis of schizophrenia by one of your doctors. I just wondered what it's like for you and what the main problems are.
Client: The main problem is these. Well, they tell me that it's a problem to do with musketsophrenia. These voices, they come and they. I heard these people talking about me and talking about how rubbish I am and what a failure I am, and I really just wish they'd leave me alone.
Counselor: Yes, that's extremely negative content to what's being said. So it's a clear voice outside of your head, is it?
Client: Yeah, yeah, it's two voices. And, you know, sometimes they're talking to me and sometimes they're talking about me, but it's always really negative. There's no helpful things there at all.
Counselor: It sounds like these voices are associated with a feeling of sadness. Am I getting that right or is that another feeling?
Client: Oh, well, when I let them, they get me really down. They get me really, really down. But, you know, I'm fighting these. Fighting them still, you know.
Counselor: What are you doing to fight?
Client: Well, there's where I get into a real problem, because I shout back at them. And, you know, my neighbors, they. Well, you know, they don't understand and they say they don't hear these voices. Sometimes I wonder if my neighbors are in on it as well, but, you know, they say that they can't hear them, but I don't understand how they can't hear them because they're so loud.
Counselor: So loud.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What do you make of these voices, then? Do you think it's part of an illness, or do you think the neighbors are doing it? Or what do you think?
Client: Well, you know, I think there was somebody once that I really didn't get on with at school, and I think it's him. And I think he's kind of got these people to be kind of harassing me. I think they're trying to drive me mad, I think, is what they're trying to do.
Counselor: That's a very distressing experience. I can understand that. So do you think other people can hear them if they're very loud?
Client: Well, you know what? They say they can't, but that makes me wonder if they know what they're. If maybe they're on it. But everybody says that they can't. And, you know, I don't know. I've tried my CPN said, you know, why don't I put a recorder on, you know, when the voices are there and, you know, it didn't pick them up, but I don't know. Maybe it was faulty or something. It just nobody else can hear them, I guess, is the answer to your question. Or everybody says they can't.
Counselor: Even with the tape recorder, you still don't think. Well, you think other people maybe can see them, hear them?
Client: Well, sometimes I think people can hear them, and sometimes I think, you know, well, maybe my CPN's right. Maybe it's my imagination.
Counselor: So is it just you that hears voices, or do other people in society hear voices, Tony?
Client: Well, there's somebody else at the day center, and he hears voices that other people can't hear. And we've talked together, and I can't hear the voices that he's hearing.
Counselor: That's interesting, isn't it?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And I wonder if there's certain types of stress which can make anybody hear a voice. Have you ever heard of that kind of a thing? No, because quite often, soldiers coming back from the war will be hearing the sounds of battle, gunfire and helicopters, etcetera. So they're not actually there, but they hear them as if they're real, and it's linked to the stress of being in a war. Do you ever find that your own voices are worse if you're not getting asleep, if you're sleeping really badly?
Client: Definitely, definitely. What I find is that sometimes when I get really worried about what they're doing to me, and I think, well, maybe I'll stay up just in case they're going to pull some tricks or something in the night. And times when I do that, actually, I do hear them more the next day.
Counselor: So maybe lack of sleep has something to do with voice hearing. And this is very commonly seen in society that the longer that people stay awake, the more liable they are to hallucinate. What about drugs? Are the certain drugs that cause voices? What do you think?
Client: I don't know. I guess I've heard people talking about being a bit paranoid when they take cannabis, but I don't know whether that would be.
Counselor: I mean, there's other types of drugs that make you see things like taking LSD or anything really nasty like that.
Client: Yeah, I've heard of that.
Counselor:
output: Can really make you hallucinate things that aren't actually there. So there's lots of possible causes. It seems like the human brain can very easily hallucinate under certain conditions, and there are certain things that can keep that hallucination going. So it seems like about 8% of society will have a period in their life of hearing the kind of voices that you're hearing, Tony. But the vast majority of them will get better again. 8%. 8%. So it's a very common human experience. But at the far end of that 8%, there's a group of people with a diagnosis of schizophrenia because their voices are so distressing. They're hearing them day in, day out, and they're really affecting their life. So that is where that kind of label comes from. Basically, everybody at some point has had some kind of hallucination, whether it be hearing things, seeing things, feeling a touch.

Am I good enough for her? Kind of starting to feel a little fearful that she would just up and leave me.
Counselor: Why were you feeling that she would just leave over something as simple as forgetting to take out the trash?
Client: I don't know. I kind of don't know why. I just didn't like the way that she was talking to me and got so upset about it. And then I figured that, you know, I can't remember to do something so simple. Why is she still with me? I'm not good enough. I don't know.Just got scared
Counselor: have past experiences, maybe played a role in this feeling.
Client: Yeah. So I told you last week that my mother passed, left me. And I don't know, I kind of feel like she could do the same thing or my girlfriend's going to do the same thing. I've had other girlfriends before, but I guess since I'm older now and relationships are more serious, I kind of see her as someone I want to spend my life with. And my mother didn't do that. She left me when I was ten and I kind of felt abandoned. And I feel like, you know, if I had a serious girlfriend, as I do now, I feel like that could be a possibility of her leaving me and me being able to try to figure my way out in life again and starting all over, and I don't want to go back to that dark place again.
Counselor: You're generalizing your past experience with your mother onto the current relationship with your girlfriend. And why do you think those two who are associated?
Client: I don't know. I guess I was getting that unconditional love before with my mother, before she left me. And I kind of feel like my girlfriend has given me that love and kind of fearful of losing that love that someone cares and loves for me, for who I am. But I guess when I'm doing something so simple or forgetting to do something simple, or I. I have these moments where I feel like I'm not good enough and she's gonna leave me, too.
Counselor: You're overgeneralizing and catastrophizing. Can you see how you're doing that?
Client: Yeah, I do. I'm fearful of losing my girlfriend, as I once did with my mother, because I felt like, you know, I did something wrong.
Counselor: How do you think we can change these negative thoughts in your head when these incidents are occurring and change them into positive ones?
Client: I don't know. Do you think speaking to my girlfriend about it or when I'm feeling these fearful acts or thoughts?
Counselor:
output: So I think that would be a good tool for you, would be to talk to your girlfriend. Anytime you feel that sense of dread and you're starting to feel negatively, I think you should also write it down and take whatever negative thought you had, replace it with a positive and write that down as well and how you battled through it. I think that would be a really good exercise for you. And I think we can come up with a couple more strategies next week. Mean, you could collaboratively work together and do that. Would that be something that you would be interested in doing?

Because what I'm going to ask you now is to imagine what the little voice in your head, you know, that little self talk is saying when you're feeling anxious. So what are you feeling anxious about? What's the sort of story in your head that's going on there?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Terry. How you doing today?
Client: I'm okay, I think.
Counselor: You okay?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I know when we talked last time, you were having a rough time dealing with the passing year, Sister Sheila.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And you're kind of a point where we were talking about emotional consequences, but also some of the thinking that's going on. Have you been processing that?
Client: Yeah, I've been thinking about some of that and, you know, trying to kind of work through it a little bit. So I think I'm kind of ready to kind of work through it and talk about it a little bit now.
Counselor: So, feeling a little less emotional and feeling a little more thinking about it. And, like, on the rational side, like we talked about rational and irrational beliefs.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: A little more focus there or more ability to focus there today.
Client: Yeah, I think I'm ready to think about it more.
Counselor: I know the emotional part was tough for you, and I'm sure it still.
Client: Is, but I think I've kind of got through some of that, and I'm ready to kind of get through the way I'm thinking about some things.
Counselor: Ready to look at through the thinking lens.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So to speak. All right. So what are some of the thoughts or beliefs that you've been having, you think maybe part of what's affecting your mood?
Client: Well, I've been. I've been thinking about it, and, you know, I just. I just feel like I don't. I don't have anybody that I can talk to. I mean, I just. I keep thinking about it. I don't have anybody to talk to. She was the only one I had to talk to.
Counselor: So in your relationship with her, you guys talked a lot. She was an important person in your life for a variety of reasons, but including that she was easy to talk to.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And that you could talk to her?
Client: I. Yes.
Counselor: So the thought is you have nobody to talk to.
Client: I just, you know, she was just everything to me. I talked to her about everything, and, you know, she was just always gave me good advice, and she could always work, you know, talk me through anything that I needed to talk about, and I just don't feel like I have that anymore. Since she's going, I don't have anybody like that anymore.
Counselor: That relationship is valuable to you, and you've lost that, and you feel like you've lost having anybody that you could talk to. Is that. Is that close?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: All right, so let's look at that thought. Let's break that down. Certainly you were able to talk to her, as you mentioned, and you have lost her.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Right. So you have lost someone that you could talk to that was very valuable to you, and that's understandably painful. The question would be, have you lost everybody that you could talk to? Is there anyone else in your life, for instance, currently, that you regularly speak with?
Client: Well, you know, since you said that, you know, maybe I do have some people that I can go to. They're not her. But, you know, you know, I have a couple of people that I can talk to that they're willing to talk to me about certain things. I guess if I give them the chance, you know, I'll be able to talk to them.
Counselor: So there are some people in your life that you can talk to. They certainly don't replace your sister, but you have people you can't communicate with, and that can be helpful for you.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So as we build kind of a rationale, self talk to replace the irrational thinking that you brought in.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Which was that you have no one to talk to. Could the replacement be something like, I had my sister to talk to, and she was really good at that, and it's painful to have lost her, but I gained something from that experience, and I do still have some people to talk to now.
Client: Yeah, that sounds about right.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: Yeah, yeah. Yeah. Because nobody's gonna replace my sister. But, you know, I do think that there's other people that can. Could help me and what I need to talk. Yeah.
Counselor: And maybe one thing that you can. You can take away from this as well is that because of the way you could talk to your sister, you are a more effective communicator now, and you can make the most out of the relationships that you have now with people currently. Another rational thought kind of honors her contribution to you.
Client: Right? Yeah, because, you know, she is, like, the only one that believed in me. I mean, she just, you know, she always, you know, pushed me to go higher and, you know, on my job. She always said that, you know, that you can do it, you know, just believe in yourself. She always, you know, encouraged me to. To go back to school and, you know, I'm, you know, I have done that and, you know, continually doing that, you know, but, you know, she was a big motivator for me. And, you know, since she's gone now, you know, I don't feel like that I have anybody else that gives me that push that she did.
Counselor:
output: So. So the thought would be, I've lost the only person that would believe in me. Yes, something like that. Okay, so she was a great positive force, great positive presence and contributor in your life, in part because she believed in you.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hey, Julie. So last time you were here, you talked about the need for acceptance and approval from your friends, especially a close group of friends that you're involved with.
Client: Yeah, there's, like, my main friends that. Yeah, they kind of. It's like peer pressure, sort of. But I can't say no. I feel like I have to say yes just. Just because they are my friends. I do care about them and I don't want to lose them. But sometimes some of the stuff that we do, I feel like I don't really want to do it. And to keep them, I feel like I need to make the sacrifice to do what they want to do and go along with it, even though I know it might not be right. So I just kind of want to build up my self esteem and my confidence and accepting myself. That way I can tell them no and they won't overreact. So I want to be able to say it in a good way. That way I can keep them.
Counselor:
output: Okay, so to do this, we're going to do a little technique that I've used before called role playing. So I will be one of your friends, and you'll remain who you are. Does that sound okay? Something you want to do?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, misses James. How are you doing today?
Client: I'm okay.
Counselor: That's good. I just want to start out really quickly by getting a couple of the formalities out of the way. I know it's a little bit awkward coming in, you know, always the first time, but I'll just introduce myself and then you can introduce yourself and we'll just talk a little bit about you and your family and all that. So again, my name is Marisa and I just want you to know in the beginning that what I do as a counselor is more important to me than just a paycheck. I'm not in this job because it's just a source of income from. I really enjoy getting to know the clients that come through those doors and I like to help them in whatever ways I can. If it's just listening for that day and there's a burden that you have or if it's. If it's some kind of resource that you need from me and that I'm able to reach out there and get for you so that you can. You can be more successful and more fulfilled and happier than. That's what I want for you. Definitely. But why don't you tell me a little bit about yourself?
Client: Well, I don't know what to tell. I mean, they. The Medicaid office told me I had to come down and to be counseled so I can continue getting my benefits, which I need because I cancer. So that's why I'm here.
Counselor: What about your family? Tell me a little bit about them.
Client: Well, I'm married, I have three children. They're all grown. And I'm taking care of my grandson, Jason. He's seven.
Counselor: Seven, okay. And you said that you were referred here because you needed to continue benefits now that you found out you have cancer.
Client: Mm hmm.
Counselor: Okay. Do you want to tell me a little bit about that?
Client: Well, the doctors have said that I have cancer again. Had it a couple of years ago, and I beat it. And now they're saying that it's come back. It's not something I really want to talk about, but I'm still working and just trying to get through the day.
Counselor: Definitely. You are working. What is that? You know, what is it that you do?
Client: I'm a housekeeper for a hotel here.
Counselor: Okay, that's wonderful. That's good. How have you been balancing that with. With getting sick? Are you feeling the effects of being sick yet? Or is it just recent that it's just.
Client: Oh, yeah, I'm tired. I'm tired all the time. You know, it's just a real struggle to get out of bed all the time, and then when you go to bed at night, you can't sleep. So I'm just tired all the time, and then I'm taking care of Jason, my grandson, and I'm just tired all the time. But you gotta do what you gotta do. You gotta get up and go every day. There's nothing. You just have to keep on going.
Counselor: Definitely. Well, that's really good, though, because if you heard a little bit of surprise in my voice, I mean, it was. I'm very impressed that you have cancer. You're taking care of your grandson, and you're still out there working, and you keep saying, you know, gotta do what you gotta do. Gotta get up every day, gotta keep going. You seem to have a lot of perseverance, and I really think that's gonna be a strength and asset for you during this whole process. And just coming here, being willing to cooperate, that's very good. So I want you to know that that is a positive characteristic. A lot of people wouldn't necessarily respond in that same manner. That's really good.
Client: Well, there's nothing else to do. You just gotta keep on going. Keep on. You know, nobody else would take care of Jason if it weren't for me, so. And you got to pay the bills. So you really. I mean, you might not understand that since you have a high paying job, but, you know, it's paycheck to paycheck. You got to keep. It's not like I can't go to work if I don't. I don't have the money, and I don't care. Pay the bills.
Counselor: Yeah, I can understand that. I haven't always had this job, and getting here has been an extremely long process, so I can empathize a little bit with the beginning parts of my life and being in school. Students don't have any money at all. I was working two jobs in order to go to school with loans. So, you know, I feel you a little bit on. On that feeling like you. You have to. You just have to.
Client: You can't, you know, I'm a choice.
Counselor: Yeah. So many people have been there. That's a normal thing to feel, to feel that way. But why don't you tell me a little bit about your children? You said. Did you say you had how many?
Client: Three. I have two sons and a daughter. My daughter's not around that much, and my sons are busy. They're busy working, and they've got their families and their own lives and stuff. So they don't have a lot of time. They just, you know, doing the best they can, too. They have to work.
Counselor: Do they live near, in the area, or do you see them very often?
Client: They live around here, but I don't see them too often. We get together for birthdays and stuff for Christmas.
Counselor: How would you rate, like, on a scale of one to ten, how would you rate your relationship with your, with your three children at this point? You can do them individually or collectively whenever.
Client: I don't know. Um, I guess my sons are all right, but I don't talk with my daughter that much. My sons are okay. They're just busy. They're trying to take care of their families. But my daughter, she's, she drinks and she uses drugs, and she don't hang out with the right crowd, and so she can't take care of Jason right now.
Counselor: Okay, so she's Jason's then biological mother. Okay.
Client: Yeah, that makes sense.
Counselor: Okay. And what about your husband? What role does he play in all of this? At this?
Client: None. None. No, he doesn't. He's mad because he doesn't think Jason should be with us. He thinks that his mom should be raising him. But Jason doesn't need to be with his mom right now. He needs to be with us. He needs to be in a good home. And even as tired as I am, she can't take care of him.
Counselor: So that situation has affected them, your husband and youre relationship? Mm hmm. Okay.
Client: Yeah, he's just mad. He just works, goes home and watches tv and goes to bed, works, goes home, watches tv, goes to bed. That's all he's good for right now.
Counselor:
output: Well, there's a lot of things that you've just expressed to me in the past few minutes that are definitely areas that we can work on, that we can try to find some solutions. And that's going to be one of our main goals throughout our sessions, is to look for solutions. It is healthy and wonderful, actually, in a way, even if it's painful and difficult to talk about some of these things. But what makes our time so effective is that we actually identify little things here and there that we can definitely utilize to bring about positive change. So we can definitely look at just, you know, your relationship with your husband, your relationship with your children. I'm not doing counseling with your daughter, but definitely at least providing you with some resources that you could equip her with to get her on the right track. And you seem to mention your grandson a lot, so that can even be a strength, even though it's an extra thing to put on the table that you care for him and you really want him to be successful. So what is your relationship with him like? Tell me a little bit about him and what kind of young man he is.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.

Client: Yeah, no, it's been good, you know, just trying to keep busy, I guess, you know, trying to stay away from using. I mean, it's not easy at times because, you know, just the pain I'm in and I just think about things, but, yeah, no, I mean, I'm doing okay. Hanging in there, I guess you could say.
Counselor:
output: So, where would you say your pain is at right now? And it's one to ten, maybe, like, changes every day, but, you know, on average, what would you say?
